the heart of the border State of Punjab, and is a lifeline for its economy. Almost 
after one year from the Prime Minister's announcement, the answer that we have 
received today is that options for financing are still being explored, and 
project estimates are still being prepared. Will the hon. Minister be pleased to 
state whether it is possible for htm to specify a timeframe by which we can 
expect the completion of the project? 
Sir, the second answer given by the hon. Minister is even more 
disappointing. It says, "There is no special economic assistance package for the 
border districts..." Sir, the question is totally unconnected with roads. It is an 
independent question to the effect whether, considering the fact that Punjab has 
fought the nation's war against terror, considering the fact that it is a vital border 
district, it would be possible for the Government, outside the standard 
parameters, to give some kind of a meaningful assistance. Now, we do know 
that there is a Border Development Fund. I had hoped that the Minister would 
go beyond that. This question is totally unreleated to highways or roads. It is an 
independent question. We have recently suffered a loss of Rs. 800 crores on 
account of diversion of commercial power to the farmers, because of partial failure 
of the Monsoon. There has been a shortfall of 40 per cent in the hydro power 
generation of the State, necessitating purchase of power from the Central 
utilities. So, Rs. 800 crores is an additional burden in the last one month. The 
only thing I want to know from the hon. Minister is this. Will we have a larger 
view of the country's security and development concerns and think of 
something meaningful for the border State of Punjab? 
Will the hon. Minister please answer it? 
MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI: Sir, the hon. Member has made two 
observations. His first observation was about the delay in starting the work on the 
Jalandhar-Amritsar National Highway. He said that even after one year from 
Prime Minister's announcement, nothing had happened. There is a minor 
correction. The Prime Minister made this announcement on 26th November, 
2001. So, it is closer to half-a-year, and not one year. 
The second thing which I would like to submit for the information of this hon. 
House is this when a project of this nature is taken up—we are doing a large 
number of such projects under the National Highway Development Project—the 
time-frame that is required, from the time a decision is taken 
2 

[25 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
till the first activity on the ground starts, is almost over two years. This is the 
normal time-frame. If the hon. Member wants, I will just give the rough estimate 
of time. Identification of a project takes six months—that means, we have to 
identify the project. Engagement of a consultant for project preparation takes 
four months; feasibility study takes another four months; preparation of detailed 
project report takes eight months; and the most delaying factor is—it is 
applicable in this case also—land acquisition; shifting utilities which takes 
more than one year—a delay of one-and-half year is already happening in the 
case of many projects. After land acquisition is completed, pre-qualification 
of contract starts. This is a very big project, worth almost Rs. 450—500 
crores. So, the system of pre-qualification of contract takes over four to six 
weeks; then, analysis is done; then, tendering takes another four to six weeks. 
In this way, a normal project of this magnitude, i.e. Rs. 500 crores, would take 
about two years, from the time the deci sion is taken, to the commencement of 
work. So, I would like it to be understood. It is not a small project that, today, 
you decide a project, and, within three m onths or four months or five months, 
things start happening on the ground. Now, having said that, let me explain to 
you what we have done since then. We have got a detailed project report, as I 
gave you this time frame. The next thing that we wanted to do was to get hold 
of the land acquistion and utilities. The project is estimated to cost Rs. 465 
crores. Out of which about Rs. 15 crores are being shifted to utilities. Now 
these are required to be done through the State Government. We were in touch 
with the State Government. They sent to us an estimate for this in 
April.amounting to about Rs. 14 crores. We examined it. There were some 
queries and clarifications. There were six or seven clarifications. It has been 
sent back to them. We are awaiting their response to modify it. Once we get 
this clarification and once it is approved, then we will request the State 
Government to do the land acquisition which invofves three to four km. of length. 
The acreage will be different. Similarly, to remove the utilities which consist of 
electric system as well as underground water and other systems, this itself, 
hopefully, if we can expedite the activity and if things go well, will take about 
12 to 14 months. Right now our experiences are that project sanctioned in 1999, 
still utilities are not being cleared for various reasons because somebody goes to 
court or some other delay :s caused and things like that. Therefore, we are now 
in touch with them. We have also spoken to the Punjab Government and 
requested them that please sent it

will come. That is one aspect. 
The other aspect is that you have said that we have talked about the 
financial commitment. We have to decide the options how we will fund this 
thing. We have three or four options. One is that it will be from the Budgetary 
provision which is not possible bacause of the type of amount that is required. 
Secondly, we thought of going to the World Bank. The World Bank said that it

Development of SSIs in Tamil Nadu 
*167. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the schemes and programmes implemented by 
Government for the development of small and tiny sector in Tamil Nadu during 
the past three years; and 
(b) the details of the benefits derived by these sectors under these 
schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES {SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The Government of 
India has been implementing various schemes and programmes in the country 
including Tamil Nadu to facilitate the development and promotion of small and 
tiny sector industries. The Small Industries Service Institute (SISI) at Chennai 
with Branches at Coimbatore and Tuticorin are conducting regular training courses 
on entrepreneurship, techno-managerial and skill development programmes. These 
institutes also provide common facilities, extension services, consultancy and 
disseminate marketing and export related information to generate awareness, 
create conducive situation and to motivate entrepreneurs to set up units. The 
Regional Testing Centre (RTC) at Chennai provide quality-testing facilities. The 
Central Footwear Training Institute (CFTI) at Chennai conducts specialised 
training programmes for footwear manufacturing and also provides common 
facilities and extension services. Under the Integrated Infrastructural 
Development (IID) Scheme on the request of the Govt, of Tamil Nadu, five IID 
Centres at Uranganapathy, Vichoor, Thirumudivakkam, Kattur Avadi and 
Kittampalyam have been sanctioned. These Centres are at various stages of 
implementation. As demanded by the State Govemment an amount of Rs. 
402.00 lakhs has already been released as central grant against a total 
commitment of Rs. 870.00 lakh. Besides these, Central Govemment extends 
fiscal support, easier access to credit facilities and incentives for technology 
upgradation. The National Small Industries Corporation Ltd. (NSIC) operates 
various schemes like Higher Purchase, Composite Term Loan, Raw Material 
Assistance, Integrated Marketing Support Programme, Government Stores 
Purchase Programmes etc. Thus, the Central Govemment is supporting and 
supplementing the efforts

of the State Govemment for the development of small and tiny sector in the 
state. 
(b) During the past three years 5955 persons have been provided training under 
entrepreneurial, managerial and technical skill development programmes, 
specialised training in footwear design and manufacturing through CAD/CAM. 
During this period a total number of 3000 prospective entrepreneurs were also 
trained. The RTC conducted tests of 33917 samples of various small and tiny 
sector products for Bureau of Indian Standards certification. The CFTI 
imparted training to 764 persons and also rendered common facilities for 179 
jobs. 151 units have already become operational in the IID Centres under 
implementation in Tamil Nadu. 146 SSI units in Tamil Nadu have received Rs. 
94.01 lakhs as incentives from Central Government for ISO 9000 certification. 
150 participants r eceived training under ISO 9000 Awareness Programmes 
conducted by the SISI and the RTC, Chennai. The NSIC provided assistance 
worth Rs. 165.91 crores to 1245 units in Tamil Nadu under its various 
Schemes/ 'Programmes. The NSIC also provided common facility services to 
2135 units and imparted training to 3293 trainees. 
Central Manpower Export Promotion Council 
*168. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Govemment proposes to set up a Central Manpower Export 
Promotion Council to encourage regulated international gateway for Indian 
workers going abroad; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether several Indian workers are duped by unscrupulous agents abroad; 
and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government to provide adequate employment 
protection to the Indian workers abroad? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SAHIB SINGH VERMA): (a) and (b) 
The Government proposes to set up a Central Manpower Export Promotion 
Council and Indian Overseas Workers' Welfare Fund by amending the 
Emigration Act, 1983.The primary functions of the Council 
32 

[25 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
will be to promote employment opportunities for emigrants, project 
manpower services that India can offer in major labour markets abroad, 
collection and maintain statistics and information regarding persons seeking 
employment in various countries and related matters, administer the indian 
Overseas Workers' Welfare Fund, maintain liaison with other export 
promotion agencies and recommend to the Central Government about 
standards and guidelines for overseas employment. 
(c) and (d) The Emigration Act, 1983, regulates employment of Indian 
citizens in foreign countries on contractual basis and seeks to protect and 
safeguard the interest of the emigrant workers. Sporadic complaints are received 
with regard to cheating by unscrupulous agents abroad. Whenever such 
complaints are received, the concerned Indian Missions are requested to resolve 
the disputes of the aggrieved workers immediately with the help of the 
appropriate Government/Sponsors. Also, the local recruiting agents involved 
are directed to settle the dispute by taking up the matter with the foreign 
employer. In the event of non-compliance of directions by the recruiting 
agents, action is taken to suspend/cancel their registration certificates. Foreign 
sponsors who violate the terms of employment contracts are placed in the 
'Prior Approval Category" {i.e. black-listed). In addition, Indian Missions 
provide all possible help to the workers in alien countries.

Khadi industries in Bihar 
†882. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of AGRO AND 
RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether any special scheme has been formulated and implemented by the 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission to promote Khadi and Village 
industry in Bihar; 
(b) if, so the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI KARIYA 
MUNDA): (a) and (b) At present, there is no special scheme formulated for 
Bihar. However, the Government through the Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC) is implementing the Rural Employment Generation 
Programme (REGP) throughout the country including the State of Bihar for the 
development of Khadi and Village Industries Sector. Under this scheme, the 
KVIC provides margin money assistance at the rate of 25% of the project cost 
upto Rs. 10 lakhs and for the project above Rs. 10 lakhs and upto Rs. 25 
lakhs, rate of margin money is 25% of Rs. 10 lakhs plus 10% on remaining cost 
of the project. Additional benefits are made available in the case of 
SC/ST/OBC/Women/Physically Handicapped/Ex-Servicemen and Minority 
Community beneficiary/ institution and for hill border and trial areas, North 
Eastern Region, Sikkim, Andaman & Nicobar Island, Lakshadweep. This 
scheme is being implemented through Public Sector Banks, Regional Rural 
Banks etc. A statement showing the projects financed and employment generated 
under this scheme upto 31 -03-2001 is attached. (See below) 
Moreover, for the development and promotion of KVI sector, the 
Government had announced a package on 14.5.2001, which is under different 
phases of implementation. The package consists of Rebate Policy for five years, 
option of Rebate and Market Development Assistance (MDA), Insurance cover to 
Khadi artisans, emphasis on improvement of Khadi products, creation of 
packaging and design facilities, measures to promote marketing, brand building, 
cluster development etc. 
(c) Does not arise.

Steps taken by the government to promote the 
Information Technology Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods schemes (EPCG) has been 
rationalised and extended uniformly to all sectors without any 
threshold limit on payment of 5% duty.

the Information Technology sector, with the exception of 
Business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic 
route.

Technology Park (STP) Schemes are implemented under the aegis 
of the Department of Information Technology, Ministry of 
Communications and Information Technology, through a single 
window mechanism of the Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee 
(IMSC).

be counted towards fulfilment of minimum Net Foreign Exchange 
earning as a Percentage of exports (NFEP) and the minimum Export 
Performance (EP), provided that the items are manufactured in the 
unit and attract zero rate of basic customs duty. Positive NFEP is 
required to be achieved in 5 years instead of every year.

computer peripherals to all units and capital goods of IT hardware

of 3 years.

manufacturing and trading for export purposes.

AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SANJAY PASWAN): (a) and (b)

(c) Government has taken various measures to curtail software piracy which

and containing the problem'. 
(iii) Government has also set-up a copy right Enforcement Advisory 
Council which reviews the progress of enforcement of copy right act 
and also advises on measures for its better enforcement. 
(iv)  Information Technology Software is exempted from Customs Duty.

NASSCOM and instructions have also been issued to various 
Government Departments to only use legal copies of software.

lndia and Pakistan in maintainino peace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRl DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) India's approach to relations with 
Pakistan has always been underpinned by our desire to establish peaceful. friendly 
and cooperative ties with that country. All our policy initiatives including the 
Composite Dialogue initiated by lndia in 1998. Prime Ministers visit to Lahore in 
1999, and the invitation extended to President Musharraf in May 2001 for 
summi,t level talks at Agra, have been underpinned by this- objective. 
India remains firmly committed to the path of dialogue and reconciliation. which 
is in keeping with the Simla Agreement and the Lahore Declaration Should 
Pakistan operationalize its intention to move purposefully towards eradicating 
cross border terrorism, lndia will be prepared to resume bilateral dialogue to resolve 
differences and enhance co-operation.

based on hostility and confrontation. The most obvious manifestation of 
this is its continued sponsorship of cross-border terrorism in Jammu & 
Kashmir and other parts of India. 
In response to Government's diplomatic and other measures, in the 
aftermath of December t3 and May 14 terrorist attacks, Pakistan has 
committed itself to stopping cross border infiltration on a permanent basis. not 
allow its territory to be used for terrorist activities, or any organisation in 
Pakistan to indulge in terrorism in the name of Kashmir. Despite its 
commitments, infiltration and Pakistan sponsored terrorist violence continue on a 
significant scale. There is also no evidence of. any firm attempts being made 
to dismantle the infrastructure that supports and feeds cross border terrorism, 
including launching stations, communication centres and training camps. 
(c) In the aftermath of December 13. may 14 and July 13 terrorist 
attacks, the international community has acknowledged Pakistan's 
involvement with terrorism directed against India, and has called upon 
Pakistan to fully implement its commitment to end cross border infiltration 
and terrorism on a permanent basis.

Recommendations of First Labour Commission 
960. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of LABOUR be

(a) when was the first National Commission on Labour set up;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) The First National Commission on Labour was set 
up on 24.12.1966. 
(b) Important recommendations of the First National Commission on 
Labour have been implemented by carrying out amendments to certain labour 
laws such as the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 (for removal of wage 
ceiling for coverage), the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 mainly in respect of the 
unfair labour practices, judicial delays etc.), the Employees' State Insurance Act, 
1948 (enhancement in the wage limit for exemption form payment of Employees' 
Contribution) Factories Act, 1948 (for making penalties more stringent for 
violation of safety requirements and provision 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2002] 
of welfare facilities), and the Employ ees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous 
Provisions Act, 1952 (enhancement in the rate of contribution and making default 
of dues a cognizable offence). 
Further, new labour laws have also been enacted for the protection and welfare 
of certain categories of workers in unorganized sector, such as the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the Inter-State Migrant Workmen's 
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, the Limestone 
and Dolomite Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1972, Iron Ore, Manganese Ore 
and Chrome Ore Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1976, Equal Remuneration 
Act, 1976 and Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986. Besides, 
in the areas of wages, minimum wages, employment services, vocational 
training, labour statistics and research and workers' education, the 
recommendations made by the Commission have largely taken into account 
which laying down the policies, procedures and programmes of the 
Government. The National Labour Institute was also set up in 1972 in 
pursuance of the recommendations of the Commission. 
(c) and (d) Some of the recommendations of the First National 
Commission on Labour, such as, setting up of Industrial Relations 
Commission at the Centre and State with powers and functions of 
conciliation, arbitration and adjudication in Industrial Disputes and 
identification of collective bargaining agent and procedure for recognition of 
majority Trade Unions as bargaining agents were not implemented due to the 
divergent views expressed by State Governments, Central Organisations of 
Trade Unions and Employers. All the recommendations which could not be 
implemented for various reasons were entrusted to the Second National 
Commission on Labour for looking into the same and making suitable 
recommendations. The Second National Commission on. Labour has submitted its 
report to the Government on 29-6-2002.

ILO Recommendation on Labour Standards 
966. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of details of ILO conventions and recommendations ratified by 
Government as on date; 
(b) whether it is a fact that India has not recommended all the seven core labour 
standards fixed by ILO such as ILO Convention No. 182,138, 87 and 90; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) by when Government propose to implement all the seven core labour standards 
fixed by ILO? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
ASHOK PRADHAN): (a) India has ratified 39 ILO Conventions as on date. A list 
of the Conventions is annexed as statement. (See below) 
(b) to (d) There are 8 (eight) Core ILO Conventions, namely, 
(i) Forced Labour Convention (No. 29) 
(ii) Abolition of Forced Labou r Convention (No. 105) 
(iii) Equal Remuneration Convention (No. 100) 
(iv) Discrimination (Employment and Occupation) Convention No. 111) 
(v) Freedom of Association and Protection of Right of Organise 
Convention (No. 87) 
(vi) Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining Convention (No. 98) 
(vii) Minimum Age Convention (No. 138) 
(viii) Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention (No. 182) 
India has so far ratified 4 Conventions (Nos. 29,105,100 and 111) out of the 8 
Core Conventions. 
The main reasons for not ratifying ILO Conventions No. 87 and 98 are because of a 
technical problem relating to trade union rights of government servants in lndia. 
However, guarantees provided for under these two 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2002] 
Conventions are by and large available to them by means of constitutional 
provisions, laws, regulations and practices. Regarding Convention No. 138, as of 
now, there is no omnibus provision in our national laws for fixing a minimum 
age for admission to employment and work. Convention No. 182 provides for taking 
immediate and effective measures to secure the prohibition and elimination of the 
worst forms of child labour. Consultations are in progress to take view on ratification 
of this Convention. 
The practice followed by India has been to ratify an ILO Convention only 
when the national laws and practices are in conformity with the provisions of the 
Convention concerned. 
However, each member State of the ILO is expected to give effect to the 
principles contained in the above Core Conventions under the ILO Declaration on 
Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and its Follow-up. India has supported the 
ILO Declaration and the principle enshrined in the above Core Conventions have 
already been implemented for the benefit of workers through national laws and 
development programmes.

Corruption in the country 
997. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKARA REDDY: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether corruption is endemic to Indian Society and manifests itself in 
poor governance; and 
(b) the solutions proposed to the problem and improve quality of life of the 
people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) The issue of governance 
including that of corruption has been dealt with in National Human 
Development Report (NHDR)—2001, prepared by Planning Commission and 
released by the Prime Minister recently on April 23rd, 2002. The Report 
points out that the institutional arrangements wherein public officials have 
monopoly power plus discretion in the absence of accountability and 
relatively low salaries have resulted in corruption in most developing societies. 
The problem is compounded by procedural and legal hurdles that an individual 
has to confront in almost every interface with the public authorities. 
The Report suggests that the solution to the problem of corruption has to 
be more systemic than any other issue of governance. Merely shrinking the 
economic role of the State by resorting to deregulation, liberalisation and 
privatisation is not necessarily the solution to addressing the problem. Prevalent 
institutional arrangements have to be reviewed and changes made where those 
vested with power are also made accountable, their functioning made more 
transparent and subjected to social audit, with a view to minimise the 
discretionary decisions. All such procedures, laws and regulations that breed 
corruption and come in the way of efficient delivery system will have to be 
eliminated. The perverse system of incentives in public life, which makes 
corruption a high-return-low-risk activity, need to be addressed. In this context, 
public 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2002] 
examples have to be made out of people convicted on corruption charges and the 
legal process in such cases has to be expedited. In addition, with changes in 
economic policy regime, regulatory bodies that guide and monitor the 
functioning of the relevant economic agents, lays down the rules of conduct in 
the interest of consumers and devises such practices that help in efficient 
functioning of the system will have to be established in many sectors of the 
economy that are now being opened up. At the same time, social monitoring 
through empowered, autonomous and credible structures will have to be 
established even for the highest of the public offices. Right to information has 
to be the starting point for some of these changes.

†1006. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of ROAD TRANSPORT 
AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state:

accidents in Himachal Pradesh during the last few years, it has become

TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI): (a) 
to (d) Increase in accident is not a criteria for declaration of new National 
Highways. However, during the Ninth Plan period, 334 km. of new National 
Highways had been declared in Himachal Pradesh. 5 more proposals for 
declaration of State roads as National Highways in Himachal Pradesh had been 
received and have now been returned to the State Government in June, 2002 for 
review based on the revised criteria for declaration of new National Highways.

declaration of a few State Highways as National Highways during the course of the 
10th Five Year Plan from amongst the modified proposals to be received from various 
States keeping in view the traffic needs inter-se priority and availability of funds.

include widening and strengthening, improvement of geometries, provision of retro-
reflective road signs, thermoplastic road markings, parapets, retaining walls, 
railings etc.

Accidents on National Highways in Himachal Pradesh 
1011. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: Will the Minister of ROAD TRANSPORT 
AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govemment have made any assessment of the fatal road 
accident? on the highways in Himachal Pradesh and the proportion by which 
such accidents have risen during the last three years; 
186 

[25 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the measures contemplated by Government to make the National 
Highways in the hilly areas more safer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS [MAJ. GEN. {RETD.) B.C. KHANDURIJ: 
(a) and (b) No assessment of the fatal road accidents on the highways in 
Himachal Pradesh has been made by this Ministry. However, an analysis carried 
on the basis of all lndia road accident data, shows that drivers' fault accounts 
for 83.4% of accidents. Other contributory causes of accidents are passengers' 
fault (2.4%), bad weather (0.9%), bad road (1.1%), mechanical fault of 
vehicles (3.0%), pedestrians' fault (2.3%), other factors (6.8%). 
(c) The following measures are being undertaken by the Government to 
make the National Highways in the hilly areas more safe: 
(i) Widening and strengthening of narrow and weak sections of National 
Highways; 
(ii) Improvement of deficient road geometry design which ensures 
adequate width, horizontal and vertical alignment, curve, radii, easy 
grades and sight distance etc. 
(iii) Road design measures which includes design and provision of good 
drainage system, protection like parapets, retaining walls, breast 
walls, railings, snow fences, snow and boulder shelters, 
rolling boulder buffer (netting) etc. 
(iv) Traffic control devices like retro-reflective road signs, signals, thermo 
plastic pavement markings, delineators. 
(v) Spreading awareness about road safety through NGOs as also through 
print a,id audio-visual media etc.

SSIs in Himachal Pradesh 
†1018. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the amount spent by Government for establishment of Small Scale 
Industries in rural areas of Himachal Pradesh under the Ninth Five Year Plan; 
and 
(b) the amount propose to be spent under this head in the State during the 
Tenth Five Year Plan period? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The setting up of 
Small Scale Industries (SS!) is an activity of the individual entrepreneur. 
Government, however, facilitate the development and promotion of SSI by 
providing grant for infrastructure development, imparting training for 
entrepreneurial and technomanagerial human resource development, providing 
common facilities, quality testing facilities and extension services, fiscal support, 
credit facilities, incentives for technology upgradation, marketing and export 
related information, consultancy, to create conducive situation and to motivate 
entrepreneurs to set up SSI units. While the development of small scale 
industries is primarily the concern of respective State Governments/ Union 
Territories, the Central Government support and supplement the efforts of the 
State Governments/Union Territories through various programmes and 
schemes which are implemented throughout the country in a unified manner 
for which the allocation of funds is made scheme/programme-wise and not 
State-wise. During the 9th Five Year Plan an approximate amount of Rs. 3662.68 
crore has been 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
200 

[25 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
spent by the Central Government for implementation of various Plan schemes 
and programmes for development of sm all scale industries in the country 
including Himachal Pradesh. Similarly, as intimated by Government of 
Himachal Pradesh an amount of Rs. 221.02 crore has 
been spent by them for the same purpose. 
(b) For the 10th Five Year Plan an outlay of Rs. 2200.00 crore has been made 
for implementation of the Plan schemes and programmes relating to 
development of small scale industries in the country including Himachal Pradesh. 
As intimated by the State Government of Himachal Pradesh, they have also

Review of the Rates of Premium on Cotton 
SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA (Gujarat): Sir. cotton is an important crop 
grown on 18 lakh hectares of land in Gujarat having an annual production of 
nearly 35 lakh bales. Under the Rashtriya Krishi Bima Yojna, the insurance 
premium in respect of cotton was decided by the General Insurance 
Corporation, on an actual basis, at 5.05 per cent of the sum assured. The 
premium for Kharif 2002 has been enhanced to 9.8 per cent and it is 
compulsory for all those who want to avail the loan. The farmers are hard hit 
by this steep increase in the premium rates which are, practically, double the 
rates which prevailed in 2001. The cotton-growing farmers of Gujarat paid a 
premium of Rs.20,87 crores last year. The farmers have to pay an interest of 
12-14 per cent on the agricultural loans, which is also unaffordable. The 
cultivators of cotton crop in Gujarat are likely to switch over to other agricultural 
crops, which would be detrimental to the agricultural economy of Gujarat at 
large. The present method of actuarial calculation for determining premium 
rates results in wide fluctuations year after year and creates financial hardship 
to farmers. The Gujarat Government finds it difficult to convince the farmers 
about the necessity for this steep rise in insurance premium on cotton.   The 
Government of India 
220 

[25 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
should work out a system wherein the premium does not increase by more 
than 25 per cent over the previous year for any crop in any year. The extra 
increase in premium should be shared by the Central Government and the 
respective State Government but should not be passed on to the farmers.

International Criminal Court 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Sir. the International Criminal 
Court came into existence on July i, 2002. This Court will be able to 
investigate and prosecute those individuals accused of crimes against 
humanity, genocide and crimes of war. The Court will complement the existing 
national judicial systems and would step in only if the national courts are 
unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute such crimes. The 
International Criminal Court will also help to defend the rights of those, such 
as women and children, who have often had little recourse to justice. Also, the 
Court will only investigate and prosecute crimes committed after July 1, 2002. 
It is expected to begin investigating its first cases in early 2003. The 
International Criminal Court is fully in line with the fundamental principles that 
guide the Indian polity. I, therefore, urge upon the Government to sign and 
ratify the treaty that created the Court so that lndia may join the nations of the 
world that abide by International Law.

River Water Pollution in the Country 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Sir. it is reported that 
with rapid urbanisation and industrialisation, huge quantities of waste water 
enter the Indian rivers. In the absence of environmental management of city 
garbage, about 30 million litres of pollutants flow into the major Indian rivers 
every day. About 873 million litres per day, of waste water had already flown 
into the river Ganga before the Ganga Action Plan was initiated. Sabarmati, a 
small river, receives 998 million litres per day, of dirty water from the city of 
Ahmedabad. Dyeing and printing industries of Jetpur, in Gujarat State 
discharge tonnes of industrial waste, including toxic substances into Bhadar 
river. Water supply in Jetpur, where there is an acute water shortage, is done 
from this river. It leads to serious health problems among the people. The case 
of Noyyal river, which flows through Tirupur in Tamil Nadu State where many 
of the textile industries are located, is another example. The water quality tests 
show that the amount of substances, like sulphate, manganese and chloride 
are higher than the permissible levels. 
Discharge of industrial waste and toxic substances into rivers 
pollutes the ground water also. The Central Pollution Control Board reported 
that the level of toxic substances like manganese, zinc, DDT, BHC, fecal 
caliform, etc., are above the permissible levels at all sites they tested in and 
around Delhi. 
Sir, all these reports point to the need for tightening the pollution 
control measures in the country. Hence, proper pollution checking and 
monitoring mechanisms need to be introduced, with immediate effect, to save 
river water from pollution.

Withdrawal of the Proposal to Privatise Cochin Shipyard 
SHRI CO. POULOSE (Kerala): Sir, since inception, the Cochin 
Shipyard Limited had built and delivered eight major ships and many small 
vessels. Besides making profits continuously, the Shipyard has contributed a sum 
of Rs.75 crores to the national exchequer. During the year, the Shipyard could 
reduce the construction time of bulk carriers to 24 months. In the ship-repair 
area also, the Shipyard's performance is commendable, and it is getting orders 
for ship-repair. The Shipyard is competing internationally and making profits. 
A Letter of Intent was received by the Cochin Shipyard in 1999 for the 
construction of an Air Defence Ship for the Indian Navy. The initial estimate for 
this project was Rs. 1,300 crores, and the Cabinet Committee on Security 
approved the same. As per the requirements and suggestions of the Navy, the 
capacity of the Ship is to be increased, and, as such, the estimate was revised 
to Rs. 3,500 crores, which is to be approved by the CCS. If the revised estimate is 
approved, the construction of the Air Defence Ship can be started next year and 
completed within five years, 
For infrastructure development, etc., an amount of Rs. 32.7 crores was 
sanctioned to the Cochin Shipyard, on two occasions. Utilising this amount, the 
Cochin Shipyard has constructed a Marine Coating Shop, equipped with the 
most modern machinery, completed the extension of 150 T Crane track, 
movable rolling of the Outfit Shop, expansion of Hull Shop by adding two Bays, 
and completed computerisation of Design Department and Construction of 
Accommodation of Naval Team. 
Taking into consideration the strategic importance of the Cochin 
Shipyard, I urge upon the Government to withdraw the proposal to privatise 
this Shipyard.

Review of POTA 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Sir, I may be allowed to 
make some modifications to my Special Mention. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI): No, only that 
which is approved by the Chairman is allowed. 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Sir, the Tamil Nadu Government 
had arrested the MDMK leader, Mr. Vaiko, by invoking the provisions of POTA. 
The fear regarding the misuse of POTA came true, with the arrest of Mr. 
Vaiko, and it showed how POTA could be misused. The opinion of the 
Opposition from the very beginning of the enactment of this law was that it 
could be misused, and that there was no need to impose such a law, as there 
were other laws existing, to deal with terrorism effectively. The NDA 
Government introduced POTA, despite grave apprehensions that it would be 
misused against political rivals, journalists and minorities. The Government 
had assured in the Joint Session of Parliament, while pushing through the Bill, 
that the Act would not be misused and that there were several inbuilt 
safeguards in the law itself against any misuse. 
The arrest of Mr. Vaiko has clearly demonstrated, beyond doubt, that 
the Act is open to misuse by the ruling parties against their political rivals. 
Being the custodian of the Constitution, the Government could not remain a 
mute spectator, when the assurance had been broken and the Act has been 
bluntly misused. It is the right time to decide to whether these provisions in 
POTA, which allowed such misuse, should continue. 
In these circumstances, it is urged that the Government consider 
either scrapping it or reviewing, since there is every possibility of its misuse in 
the future also.

Scarcity of Snakebite Serum 
SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI (Gujarat): Sir, it is apprehended that the 
anti-venom serum for snakebites may soon be in short supply as a result of 
restrictions imposed on the use of horses for its extraction, by a committee 
headed by the then Minister of Animal Welfare. 
The present available stock may last hardly for two more months. The 
process of preparing fresh serum would itself take about a year. Even if 
imported, the serum may not work, as it would have been prepared from 
different species. Hence, the situation could turn chaotic in parts of the country, 
like Bihar, parts of Uttar Pradesh and Assam which are prone to floods, that 
report a large number of snake bites during the monsoon season. The product 
and the serum ceased in last December for preparing the serum. Snake venom 
AS first injected into a horse since the capacity of a horse to withstand the 
effect of snake serum is several times more than that of a human being. 
Horses do not die but devetop antibiotics in the blood to fight the effect. This 
blood serum is then drawn from the horse, from which the anti-venom is 
prepared. There are, at least, 10,000 rabies deaths taking place in India every 
year. Hence, many more horses are needed to produce enough serum for 
rabies as well. 
Under these circumstances, the Ministry of Health is requested to 
take immediate and necessary action and measures in this regard to face the 
alarming situation that may arise at any time.  Thank you.

thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak on the Prevention of Money 
Laundering Bill, 1999. First of all, I would like to congratulate the hon. Finance 
Minister for bringing in this Bill, which is to be passed by this House without 
any deiay, because this is an important Bill, which is related to the safety of 
our nation, integrity of this nation; and to some extent, this Bill will protect our 
country from the inflow of dirty money to the hands of 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2002] 
the anti-national elements as well as its inflow to the political system as such. 
Sir, this Bill had been passed by the Lok Sabha, and has been thoroughly 
discussed in the Department-related Standing Committee on Finance as well 
as in the Select Committee. Sir, one important change has taken place in 
between. When we had been discussing this Bill in the Standing Committee on 
Finance and the Select Committee, the attack on the Parliament had not taken 
place, the ti,h September incident had not taken place. Now, the situation has 
further changed. We have to pay more attention to the inflow of dirty money to 
our country, to the political system and to the economy. Sir, what kind of 
money is coming? This country is facing a threat from terrorists. And that 
threat is also coming from outside elements who want to destabilise the 
nation. The Pakistan-Afghanistan belt has become the money-launderers' 
dreamland. The money launderers and the bankers have been providing funds 
to militant outfits in the region for a number of years. Money-laundering has 
largely emanated from the illicit narcotics trade. It is estimated that a kilo of 
heroin, 40 per cent pure, sells for up to $2,90.000 on the streets of the US, 
which is enough to buy a Rolls-Royce car. In America, after changing hands a 
number of times, the retail price for a kilo of cocaine works out to $1,10,000. In 
Europe, it costs substantially higher. The official estimate of retail drug sales in 
the US is $60 billion. That means, a large amount of dirty money is emerging. 
It is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish between white and black 
money. Dirty money. Dirty money is being used to sustain the terrorist 
network. Dirty money is being used to achieve the strategic objectives of the 
terrorists. In such a situation, we have to have more safeguards for not 
allowing the inflow of dirty money into our country and have access to any 
system, economic, social and political. But, Sir, I am very sorry to say that 
after a lot of discussion in different Committees, we have slightly diluted the 
original Bill; we have changed the definition itself. The definition in the original 
Bill was; 
"3. Whoever-- 
acquires, owns, possesses or transfers any proceeds of 
crime; or 
knowingly enters into any transaction which is related to 
proceeds of crime, either directly or indirectly; or 
conceals or aids in the concealment of the proceeds of

[25 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
 This was given in the original Bill.    Now, Sir, it is diluted in the 
present Bill.   Here, it is mentioned: "………. connected with the proceeds of 
crime and projecting it as untainted property. Sir, who will go and project this 
money as untainted? Who will project black money as black money? Here, 
under the definition, the culprit has to project this black money as an untainted 
one. Only fools will do that! None of the culprits will go and project it as 
untainted money. After going through the deliberations of the Parliamentary 
Committee, I have noted that the definition of money-laundering has been 
changed in the Bill. That will protect the money-launderers in the country.  So, 
I oppose the first part, i.e. the definition. 
Secondly, I refer to sub-clause (ii) relating to the Scheduled Offence. 
"The offences specified under Part B of the Schedule if the total 
value involved, in such offences is thirty lakh rupees or more." 
Here, we are discussing that it should be enhanced to Rs.1 crore or 
Rs.2 crores. This kind of money is coming into our country through the hawala 
route. Last week, in Kerala, about Rs.3,33 crores came through the hawala 
route. There was a big hue and cry. This money was used for anti-national 
purposes. It is now under investigation. Your Ministry is investigating it. Has 
this amount of Rs.330 crores come as such? No. It came in small components 
of Rs.15 lakhs,Rs.20 lakhs. 30- lakhs. How is this money coming? A criminal 
would ensure that the amount is split into smaller components, deposited in 
different banks and not detected. He will ensure that. This escape route is 
known as "smurfing". There is a book called "The International Way of Money-
Laundering and Practices". There is a mention about this process of splitting 
large amounts into smaller components in order to avoid the limit and 
channelise them into money-laundering. If this limit is enhanced, this 
possibility is more. They would not use the amount in bulk. They would split it, 
deposit it and channelise it into the economy. Therefore, I will not be in a 
position to support this Bill, if there any move to further enhance this limit. In 
fact, my humble request to the Minister is, kindly reduce this amount. 
The third point is relating to the powers of survey, search and arrest. 
In the original Bill, the authorities were given sufficient powers to make 
inquiries into such issues. Recently, we have the case of the Xerox

Xeroxcorp, had been making improper payments titl 2000 to get orders from

Government agencies. In simple language, it means, bribes were paid to the 
tune of Rs.3-3.5 crores in one single year to get Govemment orders. Did we 
unearth this irregularity? Has it been done by the investigating agencies in our 
country? Has any of our officers unearthed this? Only when there was an 
inquiry abroad, we got the information. What does it mean? In this kind of 
financial offences or economic offences, normally, our officers are not doing 
their work properly. They are not doing their work. We inquire into these things 
here only when we get some information from outside. In the past, only when 
there was some business rivalry between some business groups, such things 
were unearthed. Normally, we are getting this kind of information from outside. 
The information about the Bofors came from outside. The information about 
the Modi Xerox came from outside. Our officers never did their work to the 
expected level. I don't know why they have the fear. Whenever this Bill came 
for introduction, there was an opposition against this Bill from big business 
people, from ASSOCHAM, FICCI, etc. All of them were opposing this Bill tooth 
and nail. I don't know the reason. They were projecting that some officers had 
done something, and that some of them would misuse it. If there is something 
related to the poor people, immediately, the entire machinery would take action 
against them. If a poor man takes some toan from a bank, immediately, the 
entire machinery would go there and take action against him. In the case of 
economic offenders, normally, there is an escape route prevailing in our 
system. We take action only when there is some controversy. Normally, we do 
not take any action. What have we done here? The earlier Bill, clauses 15 to 
19, gave sufficient powers to make survey, search and arrest. These powers 
have been curtailed in this Bill. Now, in clause 16, with regard to powers of 
survey and search, the powers that were in the original Bitl are not there. I 
regret to mention that the present change "on the basis of material in his 
possession* and related issues restrict the authorities from taking effective 
steps to stop money laundering. This will pave the way for money launderers 
to go ahead and do whatever anti-social activities they want to do.

relating to economic offences with strict liability, where mens rea is not an

crime is on the shoulder of the prosecution rather than on the culprit. No 
burden of proofs put on the offender.

The Minister has come forward with a comprehensive Bill. We had 
discussed this Bill in detail. Unfortunately, there exists an escape route. Now 
the Minister is saying that he wants to save the country from these elements.

further. So far as these aspects are concerned, the original things should

SHRl KAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I consider it a privilege to 
participate in the discussion of the Prevention of Money Laundering Bill. 
At the outset, I want to make two general points. The first point is: 
there was a commitment by us to the international community that we will deal 
with the issue of money-laundering through legislation. And as you are aware, 
the United Nations General Assembly Resolution was passed as far back as 
23,d February. 1990, and now we are in the year 2002. What worries me is 
that Bills of such significance, of such importance should not take 12 long 
years to be initiated and passed in the Parliament. Money-laundering is a 
matter, is an issue, which affects the sovereignty and integrity of nations. It is 
an issue which affects not only our financial system, but the international 
financial systems also. I think this problem should be dealt with expeditiously, 
and the Government should not take 12 years to deal with such problems.  
That is the first general point I wish to make. 
The second point that I wish to make is this. This is a very important 
point. This Bill was introduced or a Bill of this nature was introduced in 
Parliament, for the first time, in 1998. Unfortunately, the matter was referred to 
the Standing Committee, and then, ultimately, when the Bill was sought to be 
passed, the Lok Sabha was dissolved. It was reintroduced in 1999.   It was 
passed in the Lok Sabha and then, it came to

the Rajya Sabha. We thought that the Bill was totall y inadequate and, 
therefore, a Select Committee was set up. We gave our report -- this is very 
important, and that is the second general point which I wish to make --on 20 m 
July, 2000. The Select Committee gave a unanimous report on 20 m July, 2000, 
itself, and we are two years down the line and the Bill is being introduced 
today. Now, the Government should explain and must explain it. If there is an 
international commitment and the Select Committee gave a unanimous report 
two years ago, why is it that this Government waited for two long years to bring 
this Bill to Rajya Sabha? This is something the Government must explain. 
Well, these are the two general points I wanted to make before going into the 
broader issues of the Bill itself. 
One thing that hon. Members, perhaps, should be explained is this. 
Sir, this particular Bill deals with laundering money, that is, when tainted 
money comes into the financial system and is claimed to be untainted. Then, to 
get at that money, this Bill makes the offence of tainted money being claimed, 
as untainted. It makes no other substantive offence. Let us be clear on that. 
The substantive offences are in the Schedule. And, that is why, these are 
called Scheduled Offences. And those offences relate to offences under the 
Penal Code, that is, waging war against the Government of India. They relate 
to offences under the Psychotropic Substances Act. certain offences in the 
Penal Code, certain offences under the Arms Act. offences under the Wild Life 
Protection Act, certain offences under the Immoral Traffic Prevention Act and 
offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act. So. let us be clear on this. 
When there is a substantive prosecution under each of these offences, as are 
set out as Scheduled Offences, then only will this Act apply, otherwise, the Act 
will not apply because if you have not committed an offence under, the 
Prevention of Corruption Act or under the Psychotropic Substances Act, the 
question of tainted money coming in does not arise. So, there is not going to 
be any parallel prosecution under two separate Acts. The prosecution will be 
along with the prosecution under the substantive offence. So. that is one point 
that must be made clear. 
The second point is this. Though I am part of the Select Committee 
and there is a unanimous recommendation also, what worries me here is this. 
What we wanted to tackle on the basis of our commitment to the international 
community was money-laundering, but what we have ultimately tried to tackle 
are offences far broader than just money laundering.   And, we as Members of 
Parliament seem to have a death-wish,

have done when the POTA was passed, namely, we should have

SHRI RAM JETHMALANI (Maharashtra): Sir, while I support the Bill, 
I must point out that section *3 of the Act is a typical example of bad 
draftsmanship, and what draftsmanship should not be like. Section 3 seeks to 
punish a conscious attempt to show that property, which is the proceeds of 
crime, is not the proceeds of crime. Therefore, could not this offence be 
described in a very simple language, that whoever deals with the proceeds of 
crime in a calculated and intentional manner -- to show that it is not the 
proceeds of crime — will be guilty of an offence? Then, any other person 
277 

RAJYA SABHA [25 July, 2002] 
may be guilty of abetment,   may be guilty of conspiracy, and may be guilty of 
any form of abetment.       So, Sir, clause 3 is likely to create a lot of 
problems. 
Then, Sir, I come to clause 24. It is an absurd provision. It is 
absolutely an absurd provision. When you seek to draw a presumption, what 
you do is that, a larger fact or more than one fact is held to be proved, on proof 
of a smaller fact or one of two or more facts. I can give you an illustration. 
Supposing a person is found in possession of a stolen property, soon after the 
theft. The presumption may be that he is either the thief or a conscious 
receiver of the stolen property. So, from the mere fact that he possesse the 
property, a further fact is presumed, and the burden then shifts on him to 
disprove those facts, Clause 24 has this kind of an absurdity. When a person 
is accused of having committed an offence under clause 3, the burden of 
proving that the proceeds of crime are untainted property shall be on the 
accused. The presumption is not arising from, at least, some fact having been 
proved. Merely because you accuse somebody, he has to prove it. Therefore, 
please understand that this presumption is totally unreasonable, irrational, and 
will create a lot of problems.  It will not stand the test of constitutional validity at 
all. 
Then, Sir, I come to clause 70. It has become a habit in every statute 
a provision, corresponding to clause 70, is, unthinkingly and irrationally, being 
introduced. Clause 70 says; 'when the offence under this Act is committed by a 
company..'. Now an offence which involves mens rea, knowledge, guilty, 
intention, so on and so forth, first of all, normally, can never be committed by a 
company. It can be committed by a company, provided some individual has 
that requisite guilt, knowledge or intention. Therefore, before you accuse a 
company, you have to find out what the authorities say, who is the directing will 
and mind of that company, who is the person who is in control of that 
company, and who takes responsible decisions in that company. Then, you 
must determine that he is guilty of an offence. Then, you prosecute the 
company. Therefore, if you have already to determine the person, for the 
purpose of finding the company liable, then, it is absolutely useless to say that 
the company should also be prosecuted. But, Sir, companies are sometimes 
prosecuted because companies have lot of property, and the individual may 
not have any property. So, you can recover large funds from these companies. 
Unfortunately, what has been forgotten by the draftsmen of this statute is that,   
under  clause  3  --  which  deals  with  the  offence  you  are  really 
278 

[25 July. 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
concerned about -- the punishment is not 'and fine', but it is ' imprisonment and 
fine'. Now, once an offence is punishable with imprisonment and fine, the law 
is absolutely settled, that a company can never be prosecuted, because you 
cannot send a company to jail. Therefore, Sir, clause 70 is redundant, and the 
draftsmen of these statues did not realise what kind of problems have been 
created both in England and in India, as a result of this kind of a provision. 
This provision does not make any sense; delete it. In spite of the absence of 
this provision, this law wil! make a good law.

Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R.

police has been sought. Patrolling of police has been strengthened in the Tiger

(Protection) Act 1972. The steps taken for effective implementation of the Act 
are as under— 
(1)State leve/: 
(i) State level and District level coordination committees have been set up 
in several States to prevent poaching all illegal trade in wildlife. 
(ii) State Wildlife Authorities carry out regular checking of the stock of

(i) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Office for 
wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country to 
prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute wildlife 
offenders. Anti poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL. 
(iii) Financial and technical help is being extended to the States under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant, 
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-
development around Protected areas for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild 
animals. Financial assistance is, in particular, being provided for 
raising 'Strike Forces' and providing arms to the protection staff for 
combating the organised poachers. Assistance is also provided for 
giving rewards to the informers for eliciting information about poachers 
and smugglers.

under the chairmanship of Secretary, Environment & Forests,

policy. 
(vi) Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend a 
helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching all illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
(3) International level:

Targets of Co-operative Movement 
1034. SHRI HARE NDRA SINGH MALIK: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have achieved the targets fixed for the co-
operative movement; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, whether Government have identified the obstacles in 
achieving the targets of this movement; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken to remove such obstacles? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b)The Government have not fixed any 
such targets for the co-operative movement. Co-operatives are organisations of 
the members i.e. shareholders. The Government, however, have been playing 
the role of a catylic agent for the promotion and development of co-operatives. 
The co-operative movement in India is the largest in the world with more than 
5,00,000 societies and about 22 crores membership covering almost 100% 
villages. The credit co- operatives advance about 43 of the total institutional 
agricultural credit. The co-operatives share in sugar production is about 56% and 
30% of the 
42 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
total fertilizer is distributed by the co-operatives. 55% of handlooms and 28% 
of the retail fare price shops are in co-operative sector. 
There has been a mixed success of the co-operatives. Some have done 
well while the others have not done so well. 
(c) and (d) Government have identified the constraints hampering 
healthy and sound development of co-operatives. These constraints are like; 
infrastructural constraints, lack of the resources, lack of professionalism, 
operational inefficiency, absence of active participation of members, 
legislative and policy constraints etc. The Government have taken certain 
steps for removing these constraints. The existing Multi-State Co-operative 
Societies Act, 1984 has been replaced by new Multi-State Co-operative 
Societies Act, 2002 to give more functional autonomy to these institutions. 
The Government has also announced a National Policy on co-operatives in 
consultation with States to provide appropriate policy and legislative 
framework to provide conducive environment for sound and healthy growth of 
the co-operative movement and to make it members driven and people's 
movement instead of Government run institutions.

Statement-I 
Details of the CSSs of the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying in 
Gujarat. 
1. National Project on Cattle and Buffalo Breeding 
The schemes of Extension Frozen Semen Technology, Progeny Testing 
Programme and National Bull Production Programme have been merged into a 
National Project on Cattle and Buffalo Breeding with higher focus on: 
• Establishment of mobile artificial insemination centres 
• Delivery of breeding inputs at farmers doorsteps 
• Strengthening of programmes for improvement of indigenous breeds 
of Cattle and Buffalo breeds. 
2. National Ram Buck Production Programme 
Under the ongoing National Ram Buck and Rabbit Breeding 
Programme, assistance is provided to the State Governments on 50:50 basis 
for the following activities: 
(i) Establishing/strengthening of state sheep, goat and rabbit breeding 
farms and  
(ii) Making market intervention operations by supporting wool boards/ 
federations. 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
3. Assistance to States for Fodder Development 
Under the centrally sponsored scheme "Assistance to States for Fodder 
Development", assistance is provided to the State Governments for the following 
activities: 
  (i) Strengthening of State Fodder Seed Farms 
(ii) Establishment of Fodder Banks 
(iii) Enrichment of straws and cellulogic waste 
(iv) Establishment of selve pasture for biomas production 
(v) Development'of Grassland and Grass reserves 
(vi) Estimation of area and production under Fodder crops. 
4. Assistance to States for Control of Livestock diseases 
The scheme of Control of Livestock diseases has the following 
components: 
(i) Systematic Control of Diseases li ke tuberculosis, Brucellosis, Swine 
Fever, Canine rabbits, Pullorum disease, Sterility, Infertility, abortions. 
(ii) Foot and Mouth Diseases. 
(iii) Animal Disease Surveillance to monitor the disease situation. 
Under the component schemes of Systematic Control of Livestock 
diseases and Animal disease surveillance, assistance is provided on 50:50 basis for 
control of livestock diseases of national importance and collection and compilation of 
information on disease situation. Under Foot and Mouth Disease Control 
Programme, assistance is provided on 25:25:50 basis to subsidise the 
vaccination against FMD, to protect high yielding cross breed and exotic cattle 
belonging to weaker section. The 50% cost of the vaccine is shared by the 
beneficiary. 
5. National Project on Rinderpest Eradication 
The OIE notified India's declaration of provisional freedom from 
rinderpest w.e.f. March 98. The project seeks to achieve "Freedom from 
Disease" and "Freedom from Infection" by March, 2002. Contingency plans to 
control outbreak of rinderpest, have also been formulated. 
48 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
6. Assistance to States for improvement/Modernisation of Abattoirs 
and Carcass Utilisation Centres 
Under the scheme assistance as grants in aid is provided to the State 
Government to improve/upgrade the existing slaughter houses and to establish 
carcass utilisation centres. 
7. Integrated Sample Surveys for estimation of production of livestock 
products 
Under the scheme, sample surveys are conducted through the State 
Governments for estimation of production of major livestock products viz. milk, 
egg. meat and wool.The salary of the staff employed for collection of data is 
shared on 50:50 basis by the Centre and State Governments. 
8. Preservation and Development of pack animals 
Under the scheme, efforts of the St ate Governments are supplemented 
in the preservation and development of pack animals. 
9. Fishing Harbours at Major and Minor Ports 
Under the Scheme Fishing Harbours at Major and Minor Ports, 
assistance is provided to Port Trusts and State Governments for development 
of infrastructure facilities at fishing harbours and landing and berthing facilities 
for fishing crafts at minor ports. The Scheme seeks to improve the operational 
efficiency of the harbours and increase the fish production. 
10. Development of Freshwater Aquaculture 
The ongoing Scheme on Development of Freshwater Aquaculture aims 
at popularising fish farming and optimising the per hectare yield of inland fish 
resources viz. ponds, tanks and flood plain lakes.The Scheme has been

introducing negotiable warehousing receipt system for agricultural 
commodities;

risk management and facilitate price discovery by amending the 
Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952;

1057. SHRI HARE NDRA SINGH MALIK: Will the Minister of

from unstable price of agricultural product;

67

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (f) In order to protect the farmers from 
unstable prices of agricultural products, the Government takes several measures 
which include announcement of minimum support prices (MSPs) each season of 
major agricultural commodities, undertaking price support operations of major 
agricultural commodities by the designated central nodal agencies under the 
MSP scheme and using instruments of.trade to encourage exports and 
discourage imports of agricultural commodities, etc. The designated central nodal 
agencies are r equired to intervene in the market for undertaking procurement 
operations in case the market prices fall below the MSPs fixed by the 
Government. The Government is also implementing market intervention scheme 
(MIS) for horticultural commodities and other minor agricultural crops which are 
perishable in nature.The MIS is implemented for a particular commodity on the 
request of the State Government(s) which are ready to bear 50% of the losses 
(25% in the case of north-eastern Stat es) if any, in its implementation. The 
Government has also taken various measures to promote agro export with a 
view to expand market for agricultural produce thereby helping farmers realize better 
and more stable prices. Import duties on many of the agricultural commodities have 
been increased.The imports are being closely monitored and the Government is 
determined to ensure through proper use of tariff mechanism that imports do not 
cause any injury to the domestic farmers. Fluctuation in wholesale prices of 
agricultural commodities are also monitored continuously so as to enable the 
Government to intervene in the market whenever needed.

1068. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the so-called subsidy is being given to 
support the fertilizer units, where the cost of production is higher despite the 
fact that the higher cost of production is a result of their inefficiency, obsolete 
plant technology etc.; 
(b) whether Government are taking any steps to cut down the cost of 
production of such units; and 
(c) if so, the action Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) Urea, being the only fertilzer under 
statuory price, distribution and movement control, is covered under Retention 
Price Scheme (RPS) and is eligible for subsidy. Under RPS, the retention 
prices (cost of production plus 12% post tax return) are fixed unitwise having 
regard to a combination of various norms and actuals of various cost 
elements. Operational cost of production of urea units differs not only from unit 
to unit but also from month to month depending upon, inter alia, the health and 
vintage of the plant, the feedstock used, the levels of capacity utilization, 
specific consumption and inputs cost. Average retention price of urea 
produced by urea industry is normally higher than the maximum retail price of 
urea fixed by the Government under Essential Commodities Act. Hence, 
subsidy is given on fertilizer produced to meet the excess cost over the 
maximum retail price fixed by the Government. 
(b) and (c)The norms/parameters including consumption norms and 
plant capacity have been updated recently for the 7th and 8th Pricing Periods. 
The 7th Pricing Period will cover the period from 1.7.1997 to

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) to (c) Under Retention Price 
Scheme, the retention prices (cost of production plus 12% post tax return on net 
worth) of urea manufacturing units are fixed unit wise having regard to a 
combination of norms and actuals of various cost elements. Operational cost of 
production of units differs not only from unit to unit but also from month to month 
depending upon interaHa, the health and vintage of the plant, the feedstock used, 
the levels of capacity utilization, the specific consumption and i nputs cost.The 
average retention price of gas based urea units is less than those of naphtha 
and Fuel Oil (FO)/Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) based units. The main 
reason for the high cost of production of naphtha and FO/LSHS based units is 
the high cost of feedstock i.e. naphtha and FO/LSHS in comparison to that of 
natural gas. 
Average retention price of urea produced by indigenous industry is

normally higher than the maximum retail price of urea fixed by the

Environmental action by corporate sector 
1074. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of a study, DISHA, conducted by the 
Tata Energy Research Institute; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that the study has found that many 
corporates do not take environmental action; 
(c) if so, what are the details of the study; and 
(d) what action is proposed to be taken in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) The Tata Energy Res earch Institute (TERI) New Delhi, had 
undertaken a study sponsored by corpor ate houses and has come out with a 
report entitled "Directions, Innovations and Strategies for Harnessing Action 
for Sustainable Development (DISHA)". The report brings out the various 
issues and concerns related to corporate responsibilities and environmental 
performance by different industrial corporate bodies as well as policies, 
strategies for a more sustainable model of development in the country. 
The report brings out certain important directions and strategies 
especially in the areas of the environmental governance, market based 
instruments, and for transport sector and industrial sectors such as coal, oil and 
gas.The report has also dealt with various causes of degradation of the quality of 
water, air, land and biodiversity and has suggested strategies and directions for 
managing these resources in a sustainable manner.

been reflected in the policies and regulations of the Government. The 
Government has also taken steps in the areas of clean technology, vehicular 
pollution, reduction of green house gases, etc. Various activities have been taken 
up under the World Bank assisted "Environmental Management Capacity 
Building Project" to make the process of environmental clearance more 
effective.

Cost of cleaning Yamuna in Delhi 
1089. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the 22-km stretch of Yamuna 
between Wazirabad and Okhla barrage in Delhi is only 2% of its catchment area, but 
it contributes about 80% of the river's total pollution load; 
(b) if so, what steps are being taken in this regard and what are the plans of 
the CPCB, the cost involved in the entire operation and what is the allocation 
for this financial year; and 
(c) whether any time-frame has been laid down to achieve this 
objective; if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) The 22 km stretch of Yamuna river between Wazirabad and Okhla, (which is 
less than 2% of the total catchment area) contributes on an average approximately 
310 tons/day of Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) load.This is approximately 
80% of the total pollution load reaching the river. 
(b) Under the Yamuna Action Plan (YAP) Phase-I of Government, 
pollution abatement works have been taken up in 12 towns of Haryana 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
and 8 towns of Uttar Pradesh besides Delhi. The approved cost of these works is 
Rs. 711 crore against which an expenditure of Rs. 655 crore has been incurred so 
far. The present physical progress of the works is 95%. A sewage treatment 
capacity of 750 million litres per day(mld) has been created which comprises 
322 mid in Haryana, 398 mid in Uttar Pradesh and 30 mid in Delhi. In addition, 
govt, of National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi has also taken up works of 
pollution abatement of river Yamuna in Delhi out of their own plan funds. Under 
this component, the Government of NCT of Delhi has constructed sewage 
treatment plants at 17 locations with appurtenant works.The expenditure on these 
works during the Ninth Plan was Rs. 617 crore and outlay for the year 2002-03 is 
Rs. 212 crore. The present installed capacity of sewage treatment in Delhi is 
2200 mid which also includes 30 mid capacity created under YAP Phase-I of 
Government. Apart from installation of sewage treatment plants government of 
NCT of Delhi has taken up construction of 15 numbers of common effluent 
treatment plants to address the problem of industrial pollution from 21 
industrial estates in Delhi. 
A Preliminary proposal for abatement of pollution of river Yamuna under 
YAP Phase-ll has been prepare at an estimated cost of Rs. 2018 crore. This 
proposal has been posed for funding to Japan Bank of International 
Cooperation in March, 2002. 
(c) The time frame to complete the YAP Phase-ll can be decided only 
after the project is approved. However, the Supreme Court has directed the 
Government of NCT of Delhi to ensure that the minimum desired water quality 
in Yamuna be achieved by 31st March, 2003.

(i)    Drawn up a National Plan of Action (1998) to Combat Trafficking and 
Commercial Sexual Exploitation of Women and Children and 
constituted a Central Advisory Committee to monitor it. 
(ii)        Set up State Advisory  Committees on Trafficking for the same

(iii)     Issued guidelines to the St ates for effective implementation and 
review of the Plan of Action. 
(iv)     Initiated amendments in Immoral Trafficking (Prevention) Act to 
make it more stringent against traffickers.

commercial sexual exploitation of women and children in January, 
2Q02. 
(vi)   Undertaken regional efforts, in aliiance with NGOs, to create 
greater awareness of the diamensions of trafficking and increase 
sensitivity tc victims among Government Departments, the police 
and judiciary, as well as within civil society at large.

situations including victims of trafficking.The Scheme provides for

combat trafficking in source areas, traditional areas and destination 
areas through prevention, resuce and rehabilitation. Emphasis is 
placed on counselling, non-formal education and vocational 
training. 
(ix) Notified officers of the level of Inspector and above in the CBI as 
Trafficking Police Officers for investigation of inter-state trafficking 
cases.

problem and to estimate of the numbers involved and trafficking 
routes.

1131. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Railway Reforms Committee had 
suggested in 1984 the creation of very few new Zones and did not suggest 
bifurcation of Eastern Railway; 
(b) whether the Rakesh Mohan Committee has also recommended 
against creation of too many Zones; 
(c) the amount allocated for formation of the new Zone; 
(d) whether any financial cost-benefit analysis for the new Zone 
formation project has been made; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) The Railway Reforms Committee (1984) 
recommended creation of four new Zones to inter alia provide relief to the heavily 
worked existing Zones. The Committee identified the Eastern Railway as one of 
the heavily worked Zones and recommended for creation of North Central Railway, 
Allahabad, to be carved out of territorial jurisdictions of Eastern and Northern 
Railway. 
(b) The regrouping/creation of zones was neither a part of reference of the 
Committee nor part of their recommendations/executive summary. It has only 
commented upon decision of creation of new zones as an example of mixing 
policy and implementation without examining the subject in detail. 
(c) An amount of approx. Rs. 30 crore has been allocated for the year 
2002-03 for seven new Zones. 
(d) and (e) The new Zones are created by carving them out of existing Zones, 
based on the criteria of workload, accessibility, geographical sprawl and pattern of 
traffic flows and other administrative and operational requirements, so as to 
provide relief to the heavily worked Zones and improve their efficiency. 
Financial projections (in terms of additional resource generation) have neither 
been made not it is feasible to quantify them. However, even a small increase in 
efficiency is expected to give rich dividends.

(b) Train accidents are caused by failure of Railway Staff, equipment failure, lapses on

(c) Some of important steps taken to reduce accidents are as follows:— 
(i) A non-lapsable Special Railway Safety Fund of Rs. 17,000/-crore has been 
set up for renewal of over aged assets and for safety enhancement 
works. 
(ii) Fouling Mark to Fouling Mark (FM to FM) track circuiting on entire 'A', 'B', 'C,

remaining portion of the work is under progress.

(iv) Last vehicle check by Axle Counter have been introduced over 175 
block sections and more sections are being progressively added; 
(v) State of the art technology of Digital Mobile Train Radio 
Communication has been sanctioned on some important sections 
for providing duplex radio communication between driver/guard 
and control. 
(vi) Walkie-talkie sets have been provided to Drivers and Guards of all 
trains for faster and better means of communication. 
(vii) Drivers and Guards are also being progressively provided with LED 
based electronic flashing lamps having better visibility. 
(viii) Tie Tamping and ballast cleaning machines and Track Renewal Trains 
are being used to get superior track geometry.
