sophisticated track recording cars, osillograph cars and portable 
accelerometers are being used progressively. 
(x) For detection of hidden flaws in rails/welds, adequate double rail 
Ultra Sonic Flaw Detectors have been procured. Self Propelled 
Ultrasonic Rail Testing Cars are being procured. 
(xi) At the Rail Rolling Mill, Bhilai, online, Ultrasonic Flaw Detection (USFD) 
and eddy current testing is being done to weed out rails with 
defects. Vacuum degassing is being done to reduce hydrogen 
content and thus improve quality of rails. Indian Railways and 
Bhilai Steel Plant of Steel Authority of India Limited are also 
planning together to produce longer rail i.e. 26 metre and 65 or 78 
metre, instead of conventional 13 metre length to reduce number 
of welds in the track.

Extending National Crops Insurance Scheme to fruit bearing trees 
in Tamil Nadu 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman, Sir, Tamil Nadu is 
one of the leading mango producers in the country. Nearly six lakh metric 
tonnes of mangoes are produced in the State every year. Delicious varieties 
such as Neelum, Alphonsa, Banganapalli, Imampasand, Sendura, etc. are 
grown in various parts of Tamil Nadu. Several varieties of these mangoes are 
exported every year earning the much-needed foreign exchange. In my own 
district, Dharmapuri, different varietie s of mangoes are grown in an area of 
36,000 hectares. 
But during the last few years, the mango trees in and around 
Dharmapuri district have been attacked by insects and pests such as hoppers, 
jassids and fruit flies. Over 30 per cent of the yield has been affected by it 
resulting in heavy loss to the growers. It has also affected our export. Even 
coconut trees are affected by europhyte and other pests. Some of the pests 
attack these trees from inside and for a long time there are no symptoms of 
pest attack. The growers in this region are seriously concerned about it. The 
Tamil Nadu Government is providing assistance through the Extension 
Centres to the farmers and tree growers. But the State has limited resources. 
Therefore, I request the Central Government to extend the National 
Crop Insurance Scheme to, at least, Dharmapuri district and the surrounding 
regions in Tamil Nadu so as to cover the mango and coconut

growers. Such a step would save the farmers engaged in growing fruit-bearing 
trees. I would also request the Central Government to provide technical

Need to link Bagdogra Airport with more international flights for 
promoting tourism 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, there is a long-
pending demand to improve and further augment both the foreign and 
domestic passenger facilities at the Bagdogra Airport by linking it with more 
international flights. The Bagdogra Airport is not only the Gateway of North 
Bengal, it is also the gateway of the North-Eastern Region like the North-East 
Bihar and Sikkim. The three independent States Bhutan, Nepal and 
Bangladesh, are closely connected with this part of our country. This part is 
very important so far as the international tourist map is concerned. 
The rich potential of the area like the rich natural flora, wildlife 
sanctuaries, tea gardens, rich cultural heritage, great tribal traditions, the most 
beautiful Kanchanjunga Mount are all located in this region. From the high 
Sikkim Himalaya to the Bodh Gaya in Bihar, this region is famous for attracting 
religious pilgrims and tourists. 
The Government of West Bengal, the Government of Sikkim and 
many other organisations are demanding that the Bagdogra Airport should be 
linked with international flights and to begin with international flights from 
Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh should be allowed to land at the Bagdogra 
Airport. If it is done, it would help to boost the economy of our country by 
augmenting foreign tourist facilities. I would request the Government of India 
and the Department of Civil Aviation and Tourism to pay immediate attention 
to this matter. Thank you.

INDEFINITE AGITATION BY NATIONAL FISHWORKERS' FORUM 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pr adesh): Sir, I want to raise 
an urgent matter of public importance. The National Fishworkers' Forum has 
decided to launch an indefinite agitation in i4^States across the country to 
press for implementation of their charter of demands. The agitation is being 
launched in Delhi, accompanied by continuous agitations in other cities like 
Mumbai, Veraval, Valsad, Panjim, Mangalore, Bangalore, 
Thiruvananathapuram, Ramanad, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Srikakulam, 
Bhubaneshwar and Contai. Most of the demands of the National Fishworkers' 
Forum pertain to the implementation of the recommendations of various 
committees appointed by the Government to study the issues raised during 
agitations in the past. These recommendations were accepted by the Central 
Government and various State Governments, but nothing has been done to 
implement them. 
Sir, the Supreme Court had passed orders regarding aquaculture in 
the Coastal Regulations Zone as far back as December, 1996. Yet, no action 
has been taken to implement these decisions. The charter of demands include 
implementation of the Murari Committee Report, adequate supply of kerosene 
for fishing at subsidized rates, stopping import of fish, implementation of the 
Mandal Commission's recommendation regarding inclusion of fishing 
community in the list of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and 
cancellation of licences to foreign vessels. It is, perhaps, a violation of the 
Indian Constitution to grant licences to foreign trawlers. Indian fishing is not a 
profession alone, it is our life-style; but, slowly, this tradition, which is a source 
of livelihood for many in our country, is being taken away. I hereby urge upon 
the Union Government to intervene in the matter and settle the demands of the 
National Fishworkers' Forum at the earliest and ensure that the right of the 
fishing community over the water bodies remains unabridged.

Need to tackle drinking water crisis in India 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Sir, what a problem in 
India? Portends of the impending water crisis are now clearly visible in many 
parts of India. The per capita availability of water in the country has been 
reduced to less than 1000 cubic metres. It was 5000 cubic metres at the time 
of Independence, when our population was only 35 crores. In India, around 
18,365 rural habitations are not covered by any water supply programme, and 
1,53,981 rural habitations are partially covered, as per the 
214 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
2001 estimations. Rajasthan is the State where the highest number of rural 
habitations are still uncovered or partially covered by water supply schemes. 
According to experts, about 2.5 million Indians will have no access to safe 
drinking water by the year 2010. More than 50 per cent of the urban dwellers 
don't have proper water supply facilities. Slum-dwellers are the major victims 
of this menace, as water availability is very poor there. Even potable drinking 
water is not available to more than 10 per cent of the urban population. The 
existing urban water supply scheme is insufficient to meet the problem of 
water scarcity in urban areas, as these services do not cover the entire 
population. There is a need for appropriate mix of Central and State 
Governments' investment and strengthening of the operational and 
maintenance system for effective water supply. Development of technology for 
water harvesting, drought proofing measures, and production of drinking water 
is also essential. Therefore, I urge upon the Government to take innovative 
initiatives to find a permanent solution to this very important problem   -- water 
problem. Thank you, Sir.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA) : Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Indian Medicine Central Council 
Act, 1970, be taken into consideration."

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, the Indian Systems of Medicine, ayurveda, unani, and siddha are 
the recognised systems of medicine in India. About 4 lakh registered 
practitioners are practising these systems in India. The system is simple, 
natural, cost-effective, and has proved to be effective for the common 
ailments as well as for chronic diseases and also for certain diseases which 
are otherwise reparatory or less amenable to other forms of treatment. 
Therefore, the Government is encouraging the system in this area to develop 
on their own genius. 
One of the measures taken to enc ourage the education and practice 
of the system is the enactment of the Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 
1970. Under the provisions of this Act, the Government, in 1971. constituted 
the Central Council of Indian Medicine, which has been reconstituted from 
time to time. The main objectives of this Council are: To maintain a Central 
Register of the practitioners of Indian medicine and to regulate the education 
and practice. Through the measures of registration of practitioners, the 
practice of Indian systems of medicine by people without any training and 
experience, has been greatly curtailed. 
Prior to the enforcement of this Act, various State Governments were 
conducting different courses of varying duration and title. In order to achieve 
standardisation and uniformity in education, the Council has enforced various 
regulations. One such regulation is the Minimum Standard .of Education in 
Indian Medicine Regulation, 1986, which was later amended in 1989. With the 
increase in acceptance and popularity of this system, the demand for 
establishing new colleges grew, resulting in an increase in the number of 
doctors coming out of these colleges. Commercialisation of medical education 
gave an incentive to the opening up of more and more colleges by societies, 
trusts and similar bodies. They started colleges, after obtaining the permission 
of the State Government and affiliati on from the universities. But the 
proliferation of colleges is leading to fall in standards. It was expected that the 
Indian Medicine Central Council Act and education regulations made by them 
would help achieve uniform standards of education and practice in ayurveda, 
unani and siddha systems of medicine. 
But, due to the lacunae in the provisions, neither the Central 
Government nor the Central Council of Indian Medicine could enforce the 
provisions in letter and spirit. According to the procedure in vogue, an 
intending society or trust can obtain the permission of the State Government 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
and the consent of the affiliating university and start a college. Thereafter, 
they approach the Central Council of Indian Medicine for permitting them to 
run the course for a fixed number of seats. There is no legal provision to make 
it obligatory on them to obtain the prior approval of the Central Government or 
the Central Council of Indian Medicine. This has led to proliferation of sub-
standard colleges. 
The Central Council of Health and Family Welfare and the 
Conference of State Health Ministers on Indian System of Homoeopathy 
addressed this issue and recommended amendment of the Indian Medicine 
Central Council Act, with a view to permitting only those colleges which 
comply with the guidelines laid down in this regard. 
Therefore, a proposal was mooted to amend the Act, on the pattern 
of the amendments carried out in the Indian Medical Council Act, in 1993. 
Similar amendments have been passed by this House in this Session, in the 
Homoeopathic Central Council Act, 1973, also. The provisions are: They have 
to seek the permission of the Central Government for the establishment of 
new colleges, increase in the number of seats, and for introducing new and 
higher courses of Indian systems of medicine, with a view to preventing the 
mushrooming of sub-standard institutions. 
Sir, with these words, I commend the Bill to the House. 
The question was proposed.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' RESOLUTION 
Crash in the prices of agricultural commodities and need for necessary steps 
to improve the conditions of farming community in the country 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN:   Shri C. Ramachandraiah to move his 
Resolution. 
SHRI C.  RAMACHANDRAIAH (ANDHRA PRADESH):    Sir,  I move 
the following Resolution:- 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
"That this House expresses grave concern over the crash in the 
prices of Agricultural commodities and the failure of the Government 
agencies toensure timely procurement with adequate minimum 
support price, throwing the millions of small and marginal famers into 
financial distress and a debt trap and urges upon the Government to 
initiate necessary steps to improve the conditions of farming 
community in the country." 
Sir, the subject is very important. Since a majority of the Members 
want to speak on the subject, I will try to finish my speech within the time 
allotted. 
The role of agriculture in the Indian economy is very vital and 
significant. Seventy per cent of the people are still depending on agriculture 
with 60 per cent of the work-force depending upon profession generally 
contributes nearly 26 per cent to the GDP. It has got a tremendous impact on 
our economy. If any particular area or a region has to be developed, it has to 
concentrate on developing the agricultural or the industrial field. Industry also 
will depend on either agricultural produce or mineral produce. Sir, the success 
or failure of the economic reforms which have been introduced in 1991 by the 
Government of India and which are being more vigorously pursued by the 
present Government, mostly depends on the success or failure of the 
agricultural sector in this country, because, still, the economy of India.is 
agrarian. But, unfortunately, the Government of India, except in the early 50s 
and 60s, has not paid that attention as should have been. Because of the 
lopsided policies and lack of comprehensiveness in the policy, agriculture was 
rather neglected, I should say. It was not protected in this country. There are 
so many distortions in the agricultural activity and I will come out with the 
reason for this deceleration. 
First, I should say that the capital formation in agriculture has been 
substantially reduced. I think, at present, it is 7.5-8 per cent of the total Plan 
Outlay that is being allocated to agriculture and its allied activities. With all its 
contribution to the national economy, it is very negligible. Sir, right from 1993-
94, the share of public investment declined. I am quoting from the figures of 
the Ministry of Agriculture. The share of public investment declined from 33 
per cent in 1993-94 to 23 per cent in 1998-99. The latest figures are not 
available with me. My information is, as on today, it is around 21.6 per cent. In 
general, only around eight per cent of the public investment in all sectors has 
gone to agriculture. 
226 
 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, it has got a cascading effect. The first effect is lesser growth of 
irrigation potentiality. Again, I will quote the figures. "The average annual 
addition to the irrigation projects from major and medium irrigation sources, 
which was about one million hectares during 1974-80, declined sharply to 0.4 
million hectares per annum during 1992-97. Of the ultimate irrigation potential 
of 139.89 million hectares, irrigation potential created is only 89.56 million 
hectares. And the total achievement up to the end of the Eighth Plan as 
percentage of the ultimate potential of major and minimum irrigation was only 
56 per cent." 
Sir, this slowdown in irrigation has affected the cropping intensity and 
yields and is a serious constraint for diversified agriculture and cropping 
patterns for productivity increases, for exports and for food security. Sir, this 
has created grave distortions in the entire agricultural sector and it has created 
a hindrance for diversification in cropping pattern which has affected the yields 
and quality also. It is widely accepted that India needs a minimum growth of 5-
5.4 per cent over a consistent period to reduce poverty significantly. At this 
growth rate, agricultural development would diversify into dairying, animal 
husbandry, pisciculture, floriculture, horticulture and other areas. This would 
spur the growth of agro-processing industries in rural areas to meet domestic 
as well as export demands. Unfortunatel y... Sir, unfortunately, we have been 
encouraging the growth of rice and wheat, that is, cereals, to the detriment of 
the nation, and to the detriment of the farmer. Rice and wheat farmers should 
be induced to look for new sources of incomes. As the world prices of wheat 
and rice are already lower than the domestic prices, and are not likely to fall, 
the domestic prices of wheat and rice will tend to fall to align with the world 
prices. Moreover, the world market for rice is very limited, and confined only to 
superfine varieties. As the demand for cereals is mainly population-driven, 
whose growth rate is slowing down, it would be prudent to divert resources 
from rice and wheat cultivation to high-value crops. 
Sir, the Government of India, over a period of time, has been 
adopting a pro-staple cereal policy, which has created these distortions. 
Today, our godowns are surplus in cereals, that is, wheat and rice, and 
disposal of the surplus has become a problem to the Government of India. We 
have been more accustomed to deal with deficits than surpluses. We find a 
problem with surpluses. Unfortunately, most of the people are still unable to 
get two square meals a day. My request is, the Government of 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
India should concentrate more on changing the cropping pattern, as per the 
needs of the ecology of the area; as per the needs of the nation. Today, we 
are importing oilseeds; we are importing pulses, and we are surplus in 
cereals, which we are unable to export, because, we are unable to compete in 
the international market. That is where the distress of the farming community 
has to be noted. 
So, another aspect of the declining capital formation in the 
agriculture is irrigation. The share of irrigation in the State expenditure has 
declined from 26.6 per cent in the Seventh Five Year Plan to 24.1 per cent in 
the Ninth Five Year Plan, whereas, allocation to research and development 
has grown from 31.7 per cent to 36.2 per cent. 
Sir, we should no doubt pay attention to rural development. But, if we 
can have introspection, the rural development always consists of very 
temporary schemes, which do not have an enduring benefit. To overcome the 
drought or famine, we have been initiating schemes under the rural 
development. Of course, in the sphere of rural development, we are spending 
more than Rs. 40,000 crores. But, it is not linked with irrigation. That is one of 
the reasons why the States have been demanding that the rural development 
funds should be given to the States directly so that the States will formulate 
their own schemes, depending upon their needs, depending upon the 
availability of local resources. The contribution of employment programmes to 
create additional employment was small, compared with * the magnitude of 
under-employment. Contribution of employment programmes, including urban 
programmes, to total employment, is about two per cent, and these 
programmes have not been integrated with agriculture, as I said earlier. The 
share of agriculture and irrigation plan expenditure has been considerbly 
reduced. It was 6.5 per cent during the Ninth Plan. So, most of the States, 
including the Government of India, have not paid much attention, and not 
allocated sufficient funds to the overall growth of irrigation in the country. Most 
of the rivers are still to be harnessed. 
Most of the potential of the rivers is still to be used, to the maximum 
advantage of the farmers. Every inch of cultivable land would be irrigated—this 
should be the policy of the Government, this should be the motto of the 
Government. The Government has to achieve that objective at any cost. 
228 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, I have spoken a number of times about the importance of 
agriculture. We have been quoting the example of China's development. For 
the past 16 years, consecutively, China ha6 been achieving a growth rate of 
more than five per cent in agriculture. In my opinion, it is only because of that 
that the economic condition of the fa rming community in China has improved. 
The farming community constitutes a large percentage of the population even 
in China. The higher growth rate in agriculture has improved their economic 
condition and has enabled them to purchase more goods. That has increased 
the aggregate demand for their goods and pushed up the economy. 
Unfortunately, here, the policy-framers have not been heeding to the request 
of the farmers because they have been adopting a lop-sided policy in 
planning. So, this is the state of affairs prevailing today. It is only because of 
the lop-sided policy of the Government. 
Sir, if we come to the agricultural credit rate, till today, we have left 
the farming community to the vagaries of the monsoon. We are forcing them 
to pray to God for timely monsoon so that they can irrigate their land with rain 
water. There is no security mechanism built, over a period of time, in this 
country for the betterment of the farming community. In 1998-1999, the 
agricultural credit rate was 6.2 per cent; in 1999-2000, it was 1.3 per cent; and 
in 2000-2001, it was minus .2 per cent. Unless the credit rate is increased, it 
will be very difficult to improve the economic standards of the majority of the 
people. Sir, I want to point out one of the reasons why the deceleration has 
taken place. The contribution of agriculture to the GDP is 25-26 per cent. The 
exposure to agricultural credit rate is very minimum. It is somewhere between 
14 and T6 per cent, in the morning, the Minister of Agriculture has mentioned 
in reply to a question that the small and marginal farmers constitute 78.5 per 
cent, and their operated area is only 32 per cent. Very good! The Government 
seems to be satisfied because the operated area is only 32 per cent. They are 
providing 48 per cent of the total agricultural credit to the small and marginal 
farmers. The Government is aware that most of the farmers who have got big 
holdings may not require agricultural credit, because they are self-sufficient 
and have got enough resources to undertake the activity. It is the small and 
marginal farmers who need the credit more. So, the Government should 
increase not only the percentage of total agricultural credit, but also the 
percentage of agricultural credit to the small and marginal farmers. 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
Sir, I want to mention one thing more --the rate of interest. I will give 
you the data about other countries. In USA, the contribution of agriculture to 
the GDP is two per cent, and the labou r-force is four per cent. They are 
charging four per cent for agricultural cr edit. In France, their contribution to the 
GDP is two per cent, and the labour- force is six per cent. They are charging 
four per cent. In Germany, their contribution is one per cent, and the labour-
force is three per cent. The interest rate is also three per cent. In England, their 
contribution to the GDP is two per cent, and the labour-force is three per cent. 
They are charging an interest rate of five per cent. In India, their contribution is 
26 per cent, and the labour-force is 60-70  per cent. But we are charging a 14 
per cent rate of interest from the farming community! So, with all these 
distortions, how does the Government think that the agricultural growth will be 
more viable? 
Another aspect is that, the small and marginal farmers have no 
access to institutional finance. No institutional credit is available to the small 
and marginal farmers. They take land on lease from landholders. They can't 
raise loans because they are not the owners of the land. Unless you own the 
land, you will not be eligible to get loans. What I am suggesting is, let us have 
crop tenancy, instead of land tenancy. The land-owners will not permit the 
lessees to raise loans because it will crea te some interests or something. They 
have got their own apprehensions. My request is, let us have crop tenancy so 
that the small and marginal farmers will have access to institutional credit. 
There is another aspect which relates to the minimum support price. It 
has got two angles. It never depends on t he cost of raising the crops. If you 
consider the MSP of differen t crops for the past four or five years, you will find 
that it has been arbitrarily fixed. There has been an arbitrary increase of Rs.15 
or Rs.20 per quintal every year. It was in no way related to the cost of 
production. But the interest rates were fixed, entirely to the detriment of the 
farming community. 
Another point-it is subject to correction-is that, 10 per cent of the 
procurement price is being paid to the St ate Governments. That is what I was 
told. When the FCI procures an item at Rs. 1,000 per quintal, an amount of 
Rs.100 is being paid to the State Governments, by way of one per cent market 
tax, four per cent sales-tax and five per cent rural development cess.   I have 
got a doubt whether we are providing subsidy to 
230 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the farmers or the farmers are subsidising the Government through their 
activities. I feel, it is not the agricultural activity which is helping the farmers to 
survive. It is the other supplemental income that the farmers get, which helps 
them to survive. The agricultural work will keep the small and marginal farmers 
engaged and, at the most, they will get what they spend. They will never make 
any profit out of the agricultural activities . This is the state of affairs prevailing 
in the country. There is one more aspect to the minimum support price. As I 
have stated, access to institutional credit is not available to the small and 
marginal farmers. They are, virtually, driven to the conventional money-
lenders. Before they start raising the crops, the farmers take loans from 
conventional money-lenders, with a commitment that they will give the crop to 
them. Therefore, whatever the minimum support price that the Government 
fixes, has no relevance to the small and marginal farmers, who have already 
made a commitment to the moneylenders.  Since no access to institutional 
credit is available to the small and marginal farmers, they are driven to the 
conventional money-lenders. In case there is a crop failure, and he is unable 
to redeem the debt, it will force him to commit suicide. The Government has to 
consider long-term and short-term meas ures, because the agricultural assets, 
which the Government creates, confer some enduring benefits on the major 
section of the population; rather than spending on rural development. I don't 
say that you allocate a small amount for R & D .  RuraJ development has to be 
encouraged. But the benefits derived by the community out of rural 
development are temporary. The assets that are being created in the 
agricultural and irrigation fields, should be used for the benefit of the farming 
community. It has to be balanced. It should be seen where exactly the society 
needs agricultural development and rural development. 
Today we are spending lakhs of rupees on four-laning roads and Six-
laning roads. \ do not say that you should not do it. But, can we afford to do it 
with the very meagre resources that are available at the disposal of the 
Government? They money has to be spent very judiciously. When the villages 
are languishing without roads, when there is no production in factories to 
transport goods because of the deceleration or slowing down of the economy, 
when a major section of the population does not have money to mobilise 
resources, I think that is a luxury to day. It may be a necessity tomorrow. You 
should spend that amount in creating more assets and irrigation projects; link 
all the rivers in this country; provide water to every inch of the land.   It would 
create more employment and more wealth in the 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
3.00 p.m. 
country and people would have the purchasing capacity to acquire goods. It 
would boost the economy. We don't need any graduates from the London 
School of Economics or the Harvard University to propagate all these things.   
It is a question of prudence. 
Sir, there are hundreds of works which are still pending at the village 
level. I am not against big dams. These days there is a lot of controversy about 
the big dams in our country. If it is a big project, there comes the question of 
cost overrun and time overrun. If you go in for small projects in villages, you 
can derive more benefits, like soil conservation, water harvesting, as we have 
been doing in Andhra Pradesh. These small projects can be completed in a 
short span of time and people can derive benefit immediately. 
Whatever minimum support price the Government may offer, unless 
the productivity is increased, there is no use of it. Today, the average wheat 
production in our country is 2.4 to 2.7 metric tonnes per hectare; whereas, in 
other countries it is 7 metric tonnes per hectare. Even if you increase the 
minimum support price, you cannot atta in the level of 7 metric tonnes per 
hectare. If you fix a price of Rs. 1,00 0 per metric tonne, you would get Rs. 
2,700/-; whereas, the other countries would get Rs. 7,000 per metric tonne. 
The Government has to ponder over this issue. Efforts should be made to 
increase the productivity in this country. 
Sir, our product is not competitive because we are unable to achieve 
the productivity and we are unable to maintain the quality in order to compete 
in the international market. Every country in the world has got an objective to 
address to the global needs. Our exposure in the world market in terms of 
export of agriculture produce is to the extent of 0.6 per cent wnich is very 
negligible and invisible. It is nowhere visible in the international market. Why is 
it happening? It is happening because you have neglected the agriculture 
sector from the beginning. You want to create superficial development which is 
not going to yield results. 
That is not yielding result. So, or ientation towards exports has to be 
done. Produce those which can be exported; change the cropping pattern so 
that the farmers get the maximum benefit. 
232 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, one more thing which the Government has to focus its attention 
on, is with regard to crop insurance. Of course, we have the crop insurance 
scheme. But, in our area, the people say, it is not crop insurance but it is a 
loan insurance. If somebody borrows loan on a crop, insurance is there, but it 
is to cover the loan and not the crop. So, do we call it crop insurance or loan 
insurance? Our demand is, create a separate corporation run by 
professionals, -- not by IAS officers who do not have any knowledge about 
agriculture in this country, -- extend this activity to all the crops and to all the 
areas of the country. Then, as regards the farming subsidy, to what extent are 
we protecting the farming community in this country? We say that we are 
providing subsidies to them. Is it really so? When we are unable to provide 
them even the cost of production, ho w can we claim that we are providing 
subsidy to the farmers, whereas they are providing revenue to the 
Government, in terms of sales tax, transportation costs, etc. Sir, the 
agricultural health of this country should not be neglected on any account. 
Sir, one more thing is, we have agricultural experts running the 
Ministry of Agriculture; we have experts in every activity of the Ministry, but 
persons who do not have basic knowledge about agriculture are being kept at 
the helm of affairs. And, it is becoming very difficult to give feedback to the 
Government so that they can take good decisions". Till now, the Government, 
whichever party had been in power, has been advised not to adopt a pro-
staple cereal policy, and this has caused total detriment to the country. Today, 
we are importing oilseeds, pulses, etc., and we are spending thousands of 
crores on foreign exchange. This is because of the lopsided policies of the 
Government, which will have to be rectified.      . 
Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity and I request the 
Government to initiate all these measures so that the agricultural activity, 
which is the lifeline of our country, can flourish.  Thank you.

SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Sir, I congratulate my 
hon. colleague for raising a very important issue in our country. I am in full 
agreement with the concern expressed in the Resolution. I join with him in 
urging upon the Government to take all appropriate measures to protect the 
interests of the agricultural workers, the peasants and the common people in 
this country. It is a fact that the prices of most of the agricultural commodities 
have crashed. The price of coconut, the price of arecanut, tobacco, and, 
recently, the price of raw silk, have all crashed. I do not want to extend the list.    
The prices of almost all crops have crashed. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
Because of the price crash, the peas ants are suffering, the agricultural 
workers are suffering, the common people are suffering, and the economies of 
most of the States are facing great difficulties because of the crash in the price 
of most of these agricultural commodities. How to deal with this most important 
issue? To me, there should be a two-pronged approach to tackle the problem. 
One is, certain immediate measures, to protect the interests of the peasants, 
the agricultural workers, and the common man, should be taken. Secondly, 
there should be, a re-look, a re-thinking, into the whole gamut of the basic 
policies which we are pursuing in the agricultural sector, particularly, in the 
context of the WTO regime. Sir, the mover of the Resolution has already 
brought to our notice - yes; the investments are not picking up, and there is a 
drastic fall in the public investments. The capital formation is facing serious 
problems. So, what is in store for us? If investment does not pick up, if capital 
formation does not pick up, the future is very bleak, and if you look at the 
productivity increase with regard to most of the crops, you will find that it is 
stagnant, and, as far as foodgrains production is concerned, during the last 
decade, the rate of growth has come down below the rate of growth of 
population. 
So, to me it looks, if the present situation continues like this, our 
country would be sliding towards foodgrains shortage and starvation deaths. 
Of course, the contradiction is that, even in such a situation, we have a record 
foodgrains stock, to the tune of 65 million tonnes. I am not going into all these 
details because I do not have enough time at my disoposal to go into them. It 
is because of the decline in the purchasing capacity of the people and due to 
various other reasons that are there. All these indicators show that our future 
is very bleak. 
Now, how to approach this issue? According to me, the mover of tbe 
Resolution has mainly drawn our attention to the crash in the prices of 
agricultural commodities. But this time there is a qualitative change in the 
overall situation. Earlier also prices have fallen, but the earlier phenomena 
were one of price fluctuations. Now, some sort of a permanent price crash has 
set into the system. Earlier, at the ti me of the harvesting season, the traders 
and industrialists, who purchase these crops, disappeared from the market 
and the poor, who did not have enough resources, were forced to sell at 
cheap rates. After the harvesting season was over, the traders and 
industrialists would come in. Such fluctuations were there in earlier times. And 
in the case of certain crops, which have a potentional for export, 
244

because there is no demand in the external  market, there is a chance of a fall 
price. Similarly, in the case of certain crops, which can be imported from other 
countries, if there is a surplus in the world market, there is a chance of a fall in 
price. Such fluctuations were there in existence during the last so many years. 
We took certain interim measures to prot ect the interests of the agriculturists, 
the workers and the common man. Now, after the WTO regime has come into 
existence, this has become some sort of a permanent thing. The prices of 
most of the crops have fallen and they are not picking up. Why has this 
qualitative change come about in the prices of these crops? The IMF, the 
World Bank and the WTO, are giving instructions to us. They are asking us to 
remove all quantitative restrictions. Earlier, there was a protected market. 
Because India was a backward country, we wanted protection in order to 
develop our economy. We have the past of a century-long colonial 
exploitation. Such countries do require protected markets. Such countries to 
require Government intervention. Now, because of the new regime, there is no 
restriction either on imports or exports. There is every possibility of a world 
market slowly emerging, and the price fluctuations that we face in the 
international market are also experienced in our domestic market. Because of 
the instructions from the international bodies, our Government has more or 
less withdrawn from many fields. It has retreated from many areas, and there 
is an operation of free market forces. The Government has withdrawn from the 
field of irrigation and power, science and technology and infrastructure! 
facilities. The Government has also reduced the subsidies on almost all the 
inputs. Because of all these things, the peasants are facing problems.

Government actually declares a Minimum Support Price and intervenes in the 
market, as per the present provisions of  this Bill, it will be an abuse of 
competition, it may be punishable. So, withdrawal of the Government. ...(Time-

The canteen people in the college used to say: "No food will be available on 
Tuesday night. No food will be available on Thursday night." That was the 
situation at that point of time. Now, the food situation has entirely changed 
because of the hard work put in by the agriculturists. They are the people who 
are giving food to the Planning Commission people; to the bureaucrats, to the 
coatwallas, to the tiewallas and to the safariwallas. They are spread all over 
India. But who thinks about the agriculturists? What is the Plan allocation? 
What is your attitude shown towards the agriculturists? It is only step-motherly 
treatment! Sir, I am not here for oration. I am only pointing out that they should 
realise at one stage or the other. Suicides cannot be allowed to take place in 
the country. There is no comparison between the Punjab agriculturists, the 
Haryana agriculturists, and the agriculturists of the rest of the country, 
because water is made available to them, in plenty, free of cost, whereas in 
Tamil Nadu, we have to get water from the neighbouring States. They are not 
very friendly in sharing water with us. They are happy to let it into the sea, but 
do not agree to share water with us! So, the Agriculture Ministry should evolve 
a policy that the water that is generat ed in the country could be used for 
agricultural operations anywhere, and the Agriculture Ministry should take up 
this issue with the other concerned Ministries, to tide over the situation. 
Sir, nowadays, there is a talk going on, that the agriculturists should 
be brought under the income-tax net; tax should be levied on their income, as 
if their income is very large! People say, "They should be brought under the 
income-tax net. No subsidy on manures, no subsidy on ammonia, no question 
of giving NKP to them." Like that, the talk is going on. "Free electricity should 
not be given", the Power Ministers are talking like this. If you do like that, you 
have to again go with a begging bowl before the foreign countries! You will 
have to make heavy imports. In Tamil Nadu, to tide over the situation, free 
electricity is given to the agriculturists. It will continue. Our Leader has said 
that it will continue at any cost. Kindly help us in continuing it. I request Ajit 
Singhji--whose father was a celebrity, an agriculturist himself, and very friendly 
to the farmers--to help us. To tide over the situation in the villages, our 
Government is supplying free food to the children who go to school regularly. It 
is doing so to encourage the children in villages to go to school to get 
education.   Kindly consider our request-your Department may be of

Sir, the mover of the Resolution elaborated, in a broad way, all the 
aspects of it. But the Resolution is limited to a particular point, the present 
crash in the prices of agricultural commodities and the failure of the

myself  to  it.     I   request  the  Central     and  the  State

Governments to bestow their attention to it, and help them immediately and

development of agriculture and the problem of agriculture in our country. They

implemented. The prices of agricultural products like paddy, wheat and other

foodgrains or any other commodity, the prices are not fixed rationally. 
Sir, I come from Tamil Nadu. At' this point of time, the agriculturists of

raising paddy crop in one acre of land has increased from Rs. 5,000/- to Rs.

three years. Moreover, there is nobody to purchase paddy. The agriculturists 
have no granary to store their produce. The foodgrains are lying in the open 
area. Heaps of foodgrains have been stored in the Cauvery Delta area and 
some other areas. They have not been able to sell it because there are no 
buyers. The Government should come to the help of these agriculturists. But 
the stand of the Government is, they have sufficient foodgrains in the 
godowns; they do not need foodgrains for distribution under the Public 
Distribution System. The Government has to find a way-out in order to save 
the farmers. I request the Government to look into the matter urgently. 
In this connection, I would like to say that sufficient quantum of 
foodgrains and rice should be stored for distributing to the people under the 
Public Distribution System. In the year 1995-96, the Government purchased 
coarse grains to the tune of 2.45 lakh tonnes at Rs. 360/- per quintal and fine 
variety at the rate of Rs. 375/- per quintal. Subsequently, in the- year 2000-01, 
they raised the price from Rs. 360/- to Rs. 500/- per quintal. They raised the 
price of fine variety from Rs. 375/- to Rs. 540 per quintal. The Government 
purchased nearly 14.5 lakh tonne of foodgrains. This year the Government does 
not want to purchase it because they have got sufficient stocks. So the 
agriculturists are in peril. I request the Central Government to come to the help 
of the State Government. The Government should purchase these foodgrains 
and divert the stock to some other places where it is needed. Sir, there is no 
water in the Cauvery Delta. All the crops raised in this area have been 
destroyed.   The same is the position in other 
252 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
places like Tirunavelli, Kanyakumari and other areas. It is a very crucial time 
for the farmers in different parts of the country, especially in Tamil Nadu. I 
would request the Government to come to the rescue of the farmers. The 
Central Government and the State Governments together must come to the 
rescue of the farmers and give them full support. Thank you.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Hon. Member s', it is with deep sense of 
sorrow and a heavy heart that refer to the passing away of Shri Krishan Kantji, 
the Vice-President of India, and the Chairman of our House, in New Delhi, on 
the 27lh July, 2002, at the age of 75, following cardiac arrest. The news of Shri 
Krislan Kantji's sad and sudden demise has been received with a profound 
sense of shock and deep loss in the entire nation. 
Bom at Kot Mohd. Khan, district Amritsar (Punjab), on February 28, 
1927, Shri Krishan Kantji had his education at the DAV College, Lahore and at 
the Banaras Hindu University. He belonged to the family of freedom fighters 
who believed in and practised Gandhian philosophy. He was in the forefront of 
student politics in Jre'um and Lahore. He was drawn into the freedom struggle 
responding to :he clarion call of Mahatma Gandhi, 'Do or Die', which enthused 
several of our countrymen to participate in \ie 'Quit India Movement' in 1942. 
For participating in the 'Quit India Movement', he was arrested and imprisoned 
for two years. He always stood for freedom and fought for democracy and. 
secularism. 
Shri Krishan Kantji's life epitomizes Gandhian ideals of service and 
sacrifice. He had always believed in the purity of purpose. For him, the means 
were as important as the end and, therefore, he always stood for principles in 
politics. He was on 3 of the pioneers who had spoken strongly in favour of 
electoral reforms in order to ensure probity in public Ife. He had an abiding 
faith in human values and love for social service, and had been associated 
with a number of social, political and welfare organizations. He was the 
founder Secretary o1 the People's Union for" Civil Liberties and Democratic 
Rights. Shri Krishan Kantji was also associated with Gandhian Institutions.   He 
was the President of the Servants of the People Society. 
Shri Krishan Kantji  - started his legislative career with the 
membership of this House representing the State of Han/ana from November, 
1966 to April, 1972, aid again, from April, 1972 to March, 1977. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2002]  
He was also elected to the Lok Sabha in 1977. He was the Chairman of the 
Joint Parliamentary Committee on the F'revention of Water Pollution Bill and 
was also the Chairman of. the Commitiee on Railway Reservation and 
Booking. 
As a Member of this House, he took a keen interest in the 
proceedings of this House and' enriched the debate of this House by his 
valuable contributions on social development, defence, electoral and policy 
issues on science. He was the Editor of the periodical 'Science in Parliament'. 
From 1990 to 1997, he was the Governor of Andhra Pradesh, and for 
a brief period he also held the additional charge of the Governor of Tamil 
Nadu. 
Shri Krishan Kantji was elected as the Vice-President of India in 
August, 1997. He had. the distinction of presiding over special sittings on the 
occasion of the celebration of the Fifty Years of Independence. 
As Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, Shri Krishan Kantji conducted the 
proceedings of this House with wisdom, vision and insight. His approach was 
always to give maximum possible scope to Members for the expression of their 
views and to ensure that the time of the House was best utilized to deal with 
the serious and complex issues tefore it. He also made a rich contribution to 
the high traditions established by his distinguished predecessors, by his 
objectivity, impartiality, understanding and meticulous devotion to all matters 
concerning Rajya Sat ha. Fairness and firmness were the two sterling qualities 
of Shri Krishan Kantji's character. In this age of ethical relativism, he was an 
example of impeccable integrity and rectitude. 
In his passing away, I have personally lost a guide, a guardian and a 
philosopher, who gave me invaluable advice on many complex and difficult 
occasions and situations. Shri Krishan Kantj was a fatherly figure to me. I had 
the privilege to work closely with him for five long years. I admired him for his 
astute vision for Parliamentary democracy. Shri Krishan Kantji will always live 
in our memories and guide our conduct in public and Parliamentary life. 
We deeply mourn the loss of Shri Krishan Kantji. This reference is 
made from the Chair, on behalf of Leaders of all parties, Groups and Members 
of the whole House. 
2 

[29 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
In the passing away of Shri K'ishan Kantji, the country has lost a 
veteran freedom fighter, an able administrator and an eminent 
Parliamentarian.

Question No. 221 
[The questioner (Shri Sukhdev Singh Libra) was absent. For answer vide 
pages 26 infra.] 
THE DEPUTY-CHAIRMAN: Question No. 222. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Madam, Question Nos. 222 and 224 can 
be clubbed. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: That deals with smuggling of narcotic 
substances. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Yes, we can do that. But, Mr. Rama 
Muni Reddy should be there to put his question. Is he there? No, he is not there. 
Okay, we will take up only Question No. 222. 
Utilisation of seized narcotics 
*222. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) lights up narcotics seized by it; 
and 
(b) if so, the reasons for not utilizing some of them like Ganja for 
manufacturing medicinal drugs under Government supervision? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. Seized narcotic drugs, other than opium, 
morphine, code in and thebaine, are destroyed. 
(b) Seized opium, morphine, codein and thebaine are utilized for 
extraction of alkaloids for medicinal and scientific use. Ganja does not have 
any utility for manufacturing medicinal drugs. 
SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Madam, my first supplementary is 
this. On June 26, 2002, about 450 kgs. Of seized drugs, worth Rs. 10 crores 
were lit by the Delhi Unit of the Narcotic Control Bureau. The burning 
caused a lot of pollution. I would like to know whether the Government 
would consider some alternative measures to utilise the seized Ganja and 
Heroin which are also used for medicinal purposes as 
2 
 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
pain-killers, etc. Cannot we utilise them for drug manufacturing under 
Government agencies? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, it is not medically established that 
Ganja or any derivative from Ganja can be utilised. Therefore, successive 
Government have felt that it is best destroyed. It cannot be put to medicinal 
use. Nor can any medicinal derivative be obtained from it. 
SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Do the government ensure that some part 
of the seized drugs do not reach the illicit trafficking market for drug abuse? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, I do not know if have got the 
question quite right. But it relates to drug abuse. So far as India is concerned, 
the factor of drug abuse has a very different connotation, as it has to, from 
particularly the developed western world. In our case, most of the addiction is 
limited to Opium or Ganja or Hashish. Over the years, ?cially, there is only 
limited acceptability in other than urban centres, of psychotropic drugs or 
derivatives of Opium, etc. But there is the addiction of problem. But the State 
and the society deal with it. There are very severe and stringent laws in this 
regard that have been introduced. For example, the NDPS Act is a very 
stringent Act whereby even the possession of a small quantity of Opium or 
such a drug invites a very severe penalty, these are legislative measures that are 
taken to discourage the tendency. The society also plays a role, perhaps a 
stronger one, in this. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Madam, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister how much quantity we realy need of this Opium, Morphine, Codein and 
Thebaine for our medical purposes. And how do you meet that demand? Do we 
meet that demand from seizures or do we produce these substances, or, do we 
have much more substance due to smuggling? What kind of planning is there? 
If we have still much more quantity of these substances, what do we do with 
those substances? Dou you destroy them or do you export them, because there is a 
complete confusion about the handling of these items? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, it is a fair question, but, an unfair 
observation that there is a complete confusion. There is, in fact, not complete 
confusion. India is amongst the few countries in the world, where 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
opium production is illicit. It is true that the Government controls these 
substances, and through the Government, pattas are granted. There are three 
States of the Union, where opium is cultivated, that is, Rajasthan, Madhya 
Pradesh and parts of Uttar Pradesh. The total production of opium, on an average, 
depending on yield etc., Mannually, is about 1,000 tonnes. But, it varies, and the 
figure that I have given of 1,000 tonnes, can of course, not be a figure that obtains 
every year, because, this is a fluctuating thing. On an average, India exports about 
400 tonnes to 500 tonnes of opium; export it to Europe, and to the United States 
of America principally for pharmaceutical uses. There is a certain limited 
requirement in India for pharmaceutical uses. We have, therefore, every year, a 
carry forward stock of a certain amount of residual opium. I am not giving you 
the exact figure, though if you are interested, I can always sent th£ exact last ounce 
account to you, as is available. We have roughly about t,700 tonnes of stored 
opium. We have two factories, where opium is purified. One is in Madhya 
Pradesh at Neemuch, and the other is in Uttar Pradesh at Gazi. We have only 
recently started a project — started in the sense — that H have required the 
Department to immediately commission a study. These are very old factories 
which were established during the British days, and have really run out of their 
purpose, other than really collecting opium, purifying it, storing it, weighing it, 
etc. So, how to modernise these factories so that the opium can be used by us for 
production of alkaloids or for such other pharamceutial requirements? The project 
report will be prepared for that, and I am sure, we will be able to meet the cost of 
setting up of these factories internally, from within the Finance Ministry, it 
necesary, with joint participation with one our pharamaceutical companies in 
India. 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Madam, the police and the 
various authorities constituted under the Act, are seizing opium, morphine, code in, 
thebaine, and other substances, and they have been destroying the same by 
setting them on fire. After seizure, these substances are sent to court to prove 
the case. I would like to know whether-after sending these substances to the court 
for the disposal of the cases-the authorities get back those materials from the 
custody of the court, and use those substances for the preparation of 
medicines or not. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, I must disabuse the mind of the hon. 
Member of the notion that the court keeps the seized drugs. The court has no 
use for the seized drugs like heroin. In the Court it is produced 
4 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
only as evidence. It is not only the police which is only a part of it. There is the 
Narcotics Control Bureau of the Government, and we also have a full-fledged 
administration in this regard. Do these drugs come back? Of course, they come 
back to the Finance Ministry, to the Narcotics Control Bureau, and others, and 
they have been utilised in a manner that is required or are set on fire to end this 
problem.

Norms for Maximum Permissible Bank Finance 
*221. SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India has laid certain norms for fixing 
the MPBF for the corporate customers taking into consideration the receivables 
of associate group of companies like investment made by the holding 
companies in the associate group of companies; and 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
(b) if so, what are the guidelines given to public sector banks for 
assessment of working captial finance of corporate customers/existing 
borrowers? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) Reserve Ba nk of India (RBI) had, in 1975, 
prescribed norms for fixing Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF), based 
on the recommendations of a Study Group headed by the then Chairman of 
Punjab National Bank. Over the year s, various improvements have been 
introduced in the loan delivery system. In April, 1997, norms for assessment of 
working capital needs, based on the concept of MPBF, were withdrawn by RBI. 
Banks are now free to evolve, with the approval of their Board of Directors, 
methods for assessing the working capital requirements according to their own 
perception of the borrower, also the credit needed by the borrower, Banks have 
been advised to lay down transparent policy and guidelines for credit 
dispensation in respect of each broad category of economic activity. Banks, do 
however, continue to be governed by the exposure norms relating to single/group 
borrower(s) and pudential norms prescribed by RBI.

Aircraft employee ratio in IA 
*226. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian Airlines plans to shed 7,000 
personnel as a cost saving measure to bring its aircraft employee ratio down 
to international standards; 
(b) whether the ratio will still be double of what it is in Singapore 
Airlines where the ratio is as low as 161 per aircraft: and 
(c) if so, in what manner the airlines plans to achieve this and what is 
the time-frame for its completion? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) to (c) the staff strength of India Airlines 
including Alliance Air (a wholly owned subsidiary of Indian Airlines) as on 
31 st May, 2002 is 20,605. with the current strength of 57 aircraft, the 
aircraft/employee ratio is 1:361. This ratio is normally not comparable with 
other international airlines as the requirement of the employees varies from 
airlines to airline, and it also depends on extent of operation, nature of fleet 
and activities undertaken directly; 
There is present no proposal to shed 7000 personnel to bring down the 
aircraft/employee ratio. Indian Airlines has, however, taken various steps to 
contain its manpower by freezing fresh recruitment in non-operational 
categories and rolling back retirement age from 60 to 58 years and is also 
considering introducing a Voluntary Retirement Scheme.

Monitoring of banks' participation in farm lending 
*233.   SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether RBI has decided to monitor banks' participation in farm 
lending; 
(b) whether this move is aimed at increasing commercial banks' 
increased participation in overall agri-lending; 
(c) if so, the details of commercial banks which have agreed to 
participate in farm lending; 
40 
 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) whether this will give a great boost to the agriculture sector in the 
country; and 
(e) if so, whether any concrete proposal in this regard has been worked 
out by the RBI? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRIJASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
been regularly monitoring the progress made by banks in their lending to 
agriculture. To increase the flow of lending through commercial banks as also 
for their increased participation RBI has issued extant guidelines according to 
which all domestic scheduled commercial banks are required to land 40% of their 
Net Bank Credit (NBC) to priority sector, of which 18% is stipulated for 
agriculture sector.This measure is aimed at boosting the agriculture sector in the 
country. 
(e) RBI has formulated a time-frame of two years within which both 
public and private sector banks should achieve this target of 18% for landing 
to agriculture. Accordingly, banks have beeifcadvised to take necessary steps 
so as to reach this target by March, 2003. In addition, RBI has also taken the 
following steps for increasing the flow of credit to agriculture sector: 
• Formulating of Special Agricultural Credit Plans by public sector banks 
with a view to achieve distinct and marked improvement; 
• Opening of atleast one specialized agricultural finance branch by all 
scheduled commercial banks in each State; 
• Introduction has issue of Kisan Credit Cards for farmers; 
• Setting up of rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) to assist State 
Government in quick completion of rural infrastructural projects; 
• Introduction of a scheme for financing agri-clinics and agri-business centres 
to accelerate the process of technology transfer to agriculture and providing 
supplementary sources of input supply and services; 
• Introduction of a scheme for financing small and marginal farmers for 
purchase of land for agricultural purposes; 
• Increasing the limit for financing of distribution of inputs for allied 
activities to Rs. 25 lakhs; and 
• Increasing the credit limit for produce (marketing) loan to Rs. 5 lakh.

Trade in psychotropic substances 
*234.    DR.AKHILESHDAS- 
SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the reports of 
on-line illegal trading to psychotropic substances, smuggling of drugs and 
opium; 
(b) it so, the modus operandi adopted for such illicit trade in 
psychotropic substances and seizures, if any made on the basis of 
investigations made into such reports; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to prevent the illicit trade? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) Yes. Sir. 
(b) Investigations revealed that the modus operandi was to get orders 
for drugs, mainly psychotropic, through the web sites on the Internet and to 
make the despatches against such orders through EMS speed post to the 
clients in foreign countries by mislabelling the contents to escape the 
Customs. Payments for the drugs were received through credit cards. Only 
one case of on-line illegal trading of psychotropic has been detected so far in 
which 4 persons were arrested and 2654 tablets of various controlled 
psychotropic substances were seized. 
(c) Misuse of the Internet to provide and sell drugs is an important 
issued the world over and the 20th Session of UN General Assembly 
recommended action at the State, regional and international levels to tackle 
the menace. This issue was also di scussed at the 45 Session of the 
Commission on Narcotics Drugs held in Vienna in March, 2002. The 
Government of India is also seized the problems and has asked the 
enforcement agencies to keep a close watch on such activities with a view to 
adequately combating the problem.

1376. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that India has sought assistance from the World Trade

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) At the Fourth 
Ministerial Conference of the WTO held at Doha, the members confirmed that 
technical cooperation and capacity building are core elements of the 
development dimension of the multilateral trading system. It was decided to 
develop a plan to ensure long term, secure and predictable funding for the 
WTO technical assistance activities. Pursuant to the mandate contained in the 
Doha Ministerial Declaration, the General Council decided to convene a 
Pledging Conference and also to create the Doha Development Agenda 
Global Trust Fund. In the Pledging Conference held on 11th March, 2002, the 
member governments pledged to the Global Trust Fund an amount of over 30 
million Swiss Francs for the WTO to conduct the technical assistance and 
capacity building activities for the developing countries for their constructive 
and fruitful participation in the Doha Work Programme. 
The Coordinated WTO Secretariat Annual Technical Assistance Plan 2002, 
which is being implemented lists various technical assistance activities for the 
developing countries including LDCs. 
For India, the activities listed included Technical Missions on Trade and 
Competition Policy, Trade and Investment (in cooperation with the 
UNCTAD), Trade Facilitation, Integrated Data Base, Services, Intensive 
Training Course for Asia and Pacific Region to be organised in New Delhi (in 
cooperation with the UNCTAD) and a Regional Workshop on SPS

1377.SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the new strategy of developing Commerce and Industry in North-
Eastern State; 
(b) the success in opening up the commercial water routes of 
Brahmaputra via Bangladesh and land routes by Stilwell road to Myanmar, Moreh 
route to Myanmar and Dawki route to Bangladesh; and 
(c) what is the volume of trade both way during the last three years 
through these routes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) The strategy of 
developing commerce and industry in the North-Eastern States involves inter 
alia. 
(i) entering into bilateral joint cooperation projects between India and 
Myanmar, India and Bangladesh 
(ii) entering into trilateral cooperation on developing highway linkages 
between India, Myanmar and Thiland 
(iii) providing financial assistance to the North-Eastern States for 
developing infrastructure for exports 
(iv) providing transport assistant for export of specified agricultural and 
processed products from the North-Eastern States including Sikkim 
(v) organising seminars, workshops, fairs and buyer-sellers meeting for 
improving trade with the neighbouring countries. 
(b) The commercial water routes of Brahmakumar via Bangladesh are 
utilised under the auspices of the India-Bangladesh Protocol on Inland Wafer 
Transit and Trade (IWTT) which provides for movement of goods through 
inland waterways through identified routes including the river Brahmaputra. 
As per the IWTT Protocol, eight ports-or call have been identified including 
river Brahmaputra. The Government of India has proposed increasing the 
number of ports-of-call under the Protocol on IWTT. Discussions are being 
held for the same. 
86 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The Dawki land route in Meghalayya connecting to Tamable in 
Bangladesh is in operation. Large quantities of coal, limestone and other goods 
are being exported to Bangladesh through this route. The Government of 
India is working on improving infrastructure facilities to promote further 
economic and commercial linkages between India and Bangladesh. 
At present there is no proposal regarding revival of Still well/Ledo road 
with Government of India. 
Regarding the Moreh route, the upgradation of Tamu-Kalewa-Kalemyo 
(TKK) road was completed. It was inaugurated in February, 2001: The road 
starts from the India-Myanmar border (near Moreh in India) and links up with 
the highway to Mandalay. It thus had the potential of becoming an extension of 
National Highway-39 from Imphal to Myanmar. In due course, it would 
provide the linkage for movement beyond Myanmar as part of the proposed 
Tans-Asia Highway. Therefore, the road is expected to serve the interests of 
promoting trade the travel linkages between the North-East and Myanmar; and 
in future with South-East Asia. 
(c) Volume of trade specific to each route is not being maintained.

Competitiveness of industrial groups 
†1384. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are considering to take steps to 
make industrial groups more competitive at the international level; 
(b) if so, whether Government have taken any steps in this regard;  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) to (d) The Government's 
approach to industrial sector growth and development is that of increasing 
efficiency and competitiveness of the Indian industry to enable them to stand 
on their own in the face of global competition. This approach is manifested in 
the broad strategy enunciated in the Union Budget 2002-2003, which lays 
emphasis on deepening structural reforms and regeneration of industrial sector. 
In pursuance of this approach and strategy, Government has initiated several 
measures which are mentioned below:— 
• The Union Budget 2002-2003 has made allocations towards some of the 
major schemes, which will strengthen infrastructure and boost 
demand especially in construction housing steel and cement sectors. 
These schemes include PM's Gram Sadak Yojana, Infrastructure 
Equity Fund, Urban Reform Incentive Fund, City Challenge Fund, 
are Accelerated Power Development Reform Programme. 
• DIPP has entrusted sector-wise studies in respect of capital goods, pulp and 
paper and cement industries to organisations of international repute 
with a view to assess global competitiveness of these industries. 
• The Administrative Price Mechanism (APM) in the petroleum sector 
has been dismantled w.e.f. 1.04.2002. The market forces will now 
determine the prices in the petroleum sector. 
• To deal with the forces of competition, industrial and other 
companies require restructuring on a continuous basis. For this 
purpose it is essential to promote ou t of court mechanisms for timely 
and transparent corporate debt restructuring of viable debt entities. A 
mechanism for Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) has been set up 
under the guidelines issued by the RBI. 
• To improve the operating environment of the companies and to 
improve business confidence, the Companies Act has been amended 
to allow buyback of shares, by the companies. 
• To deepen reforms in stock exchanges and to provide protection 
92 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
to the investors, Union Budget 2002-2003 proposes amendments inSEBI 
Act 1992. 
• The draft Electricity Bill has been introduced in the Parliament for 
facilitating comprehensive power sector reforms. 
• The Competition Bill has been introduced in the Parliament for 
promoting competition and curbing monopoly. 
• The RBI has cut Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to 5 per cent from 5.5 
per cent a move that is likely to release Rs. 5000 crores to banks for 
lending.This move will ease the liquidity position further. 
• The Reserve Bank has also announced measures for stepping up 
growth momentum with stimulus to agriculture, housing, small-scale 
sector and exports in its credit policy for 2002-03. It also aims at 
facilitating better credit delivery and moving forward with structural 
reforms. 
• Power sector reforms have received a boost in pursuance of the centre's 
decision to provide grants equal to the amount by which States have 
been able to reduce their power sector deficits. The States of Haryana, 
Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh have been able to reduce losses in the 
past couple of years. These three States will now be eligible for 
matching grant under the Accelerated Power Development and Reform 
Programme (APDRP).

Income Tax exemption on Income from VRS 
1399.SHRIYADLAPATI VENKAT RAO:                 
  SHRIMATIVANGA GEETHA: 
  SHRI C. RAMACHNDRAIAH:  
SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA:  
SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH:       
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "VRS Income exempted from Tax" which appeared in "Deccan 
Chronicle (English) on 21 st June, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the employees who retired from the bank service under VRS 
on 31 March 2001 and payment made during April-December, 2001 are also 
exempted from tax; 
.(d) if so, the details thereof, if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether the Ministry of Finance propose to give tax exemption to such 
bank employees from VRS income; and 
(f) whether any modifications amending rules are likely to be issued by 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. 
Through Notification No. 151/2002 dated 19-06-2002, Rule 2BA of 
Income-tax Rules has been amended to provide that amount received by an 
employee of a notified institution having importance throughout India or in any 
State or States, at the time of his voluntary retirement shall be exempt if the 
scheme of voluntary retirements is framed in accordance with the conditions 
prescribed in the said Rule 2BA. These conditions, inter alia, stipulated that the 
employees must have completed 10 years of service or 40 years of age, etc. the 
exemption, however, would be available only to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs as 
provided in section 10(10C) of the Income-tax Act. The whole of VRS income 
received by the employees would, therefore, be not exempt from tax. 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
(c) to (f) The income fr om voluntary retirement scheme including of 
employees of banking companies is already exempt upto Rs. 5 lakhs subject 
to the conditions laid down in Rule 2BA of the Income-tax Rules. There is no 
proposal under consideration to increase this Limit.

1409. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that trading in Government Securities are not 
allowed in stock Exchanges across the counter in a transparent manner on 
screen and in a demutualised form; 
(b) if so, the present practice of trade in G-secs and details arising 
thereof; 
(c) whether the present practice does not have inbuilt safeguards against 
fraud as revealed in the Home Trade case; 
(d) if so, whether any changes are being contemplated in the present practice 
and introuduce trade under across the counter transactions in the exchanges; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and the tentative schedule in this 
regard? 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFARIS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) and (b) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has intimated that transactions in Government 
securities can take place in the following ways: 
1. Over The Counter (OTC) market: Deals are contracted either directly 
between participants or through the medium of a broker. RBI regulated 
entities such as banks, primary dealers, financial institutions, etc. can 
only use the services of brokers registered with the NSE, BSE or 
OTCEI. 
2. Negotiated Dealing System (NDS): With effect from February 15, 2002, 
NDS has been operationalised. NDS is a screen based system set-up 
by RBI that not only ensures transparency but also enables settlement 
in RBI either directly beyond a limit or through Clearing Corporation 
of India Limited. (CCIL). 
3. Stock Exchanges : The exchanges provide both screen based order 
given trading (i.e., continuous) or negotiated market in Government 
securities. 
(c) The transactions unertaken by certain cooperative banks dealing 
with Home Trade show that the concerned cooperative banks had violated 
the RBI regulations and guidelines. Where the settlement is directly in the 
books of the RBI, the Delivery Versus Payment (DVP) system ensures 
that transfer of funds does not take place unless there is delivery of 
securities and wee versa. 
The Home Trade transactions purportedly relate to buying of 
Government securities in physical form. In the absence of any delivery of 
transfer of securities for month together, such transactions tantamount to making 
a clean advance in the guise of securities transactions. 
(d) and (e) In the light of recent fraudulent transactions in the guise 
of Government securities transactions in physical format by a few co 
operative banks with the help of some broker entities, RBI proposd to 
accelerate the measures under contemplation for further reducing the 
scope for trading in physical form., RBI, thus issued a circular on 
"Transactions in Government securities" on 20th May, 2002, taking the 
following measures to expedite convers ion if all Government securities 
into demat modes: 
(i) All RBI regulated entities [including Financial Institutions (FIs), 
122 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Primary Dealers (PDs), cooperative banks, RRBs, Local Area Banks 
(LABs), Non Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)] were advised to 
undertake purchase/sales transactions with efect from July 1, 2002 
compulsorily through Subsidiary General Ledger (SGL)/Constituent 
Subsidiary General Ledger (CSGL)/demat accounts. 
(ii) All RBI regulated entities were advised to mandatorily hold their 
investments in Government securities in SGL/CSGL account or in a 
demat account with depositories. 
(iii) All RBI regulated entities were prohibited from undertaking any 
transactions in physical form with any broker. 
(iv) It was specifically indicated that the custodians providing SGL or demat 
facility must ensure clear funds in the buyer's account and sufficient 
securities in the seller's account before putting through a transaction. 
RBI has further taken following additional measures to help strengthen 
the capabilities of institutions in avoiding recourse to frauds in their operations: 
(i) Urban Co-operative Banks have been prohibited from dealing with 
borkers on principal to principal basis, (ii) Prompt punitive action has 
been taken against defaulting banks and officials including suppression of 
Boards, levying of penalties and criminal action against officials, (iii) 
Cases where brokers appeared to be involved in price manipulation and other 
undesirable practices have been referred to SEBI. 
(iv) List of 'Dos and Don'ts finalised by the Primary Dealers' Association 
of India for transaction in Government securities including 
conducting due diligence on the broker's track record and 
antecedents, etc., has ben forwarded in all RBI regulated entities, 
Ministry of Finance, Central/Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, 
Secretary, Ministry of Labour, Government of India for wider 
dissemination. 
(v) Negotiated Dealing System (NDS), a screen based system setup by RBI 
was operationalised with effect from February 15,2002, to ensure 
transparency and enable settlement in RBI either directly or through 
Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL).
